title: Support pinning/managing a custom runc binary (bundled runc's masked-path mount fails on older kernels)
body:
## Summary

k0s bundles and unconditionally re-stages its own `runc` binary at `/var/lib/k0s/bin/runc` on every install/start, with no supported way to pin an alternate version or opt out of this management. On older kernels, the bundled `runc` fails because it relies on a `tmpfs` masked-path mount technique (`nr_blocks=1,nr_inodes=1`) that isn't supported there.

## Environment / observed behavior

- Fleet of legacy hosts running an older LTS kernel line, bumped to 4.4 (the newest available via the distro's own backport path) specifically to meet a runtime-security agent's minimum kernel requirement.
- With k0s's bundled `runc`, worker/controller nodes fail to start containers with a masked-path mount error on this kernel.
- Manually swapping in `runc` v1.2.9 (which predates the masking technique) at `/var/lib/k0s/bin/runc` fixes it completely — confirmed stable in production across dozens of hosts.
- However, **k0s re-stages its own bundled runc on every start**, silently reverting the fix. Confirmed this happens more than once per lifecycle: once immediately at install, and again some seconds after control-plane readiness on a controller+worker node (timing varies with host load, observed ~8-10s on an otherwise-idle host). There's no config option to tell k0s "don't manage runc" or "use this specific runc binary."

## Current workaround (fragile)

We run a small always-on daemon, triggered on every `k0scontroller`/`k0sworker` start (not a one-shot post-install hook), that polls the runc binary's checksum and re-swaps it whenever k0s overwrites it. A one-shot swap-after-install approach was tried first and missed the later re-stage entirely. This works but is a real hack around the absence of first-class support, and cost significant time to discover and get right.

## Feature request

Either of these would remove the need for the workaround:

1. A config option (e.g. under `spec.k0s.config.spec.workerProfiles`, or a top-level key) to point k0s at a specific runc binary path/version instead of always using the bundled one — similar in spirit to how `k0sctl`'s `k0sBinaryPath` lets you bring your own k0s binary.
2. Or, at minimum, a way to disable k0s's own runc management entirely (skip re-staging if a runc binary already exists at the target path), so external tooling can manage it without fighting k0s's own reconciliation on every start.

Happy to provide more detail on the exact masked-path mount failure if useful (kernel 4.4; bundled runc version failed, v1.2.9 confirmed working).

title: Reduce allocations in command suggestion edit distance calculation
body:
## Optimize Levenshtein distance calculation used by command suggestions

### Description

The current implementation of `ld` in `cobra.go` calculates Levenshtein distance using a full two-dimensional DP matrix.

`SuggestionsFor` calls this function when suggesting commands after an invalid command is entered. Since this calculation may be performed against multiple commands, the temporary allocations from the full matrix can add up.

The current implementation has `O(n*m)` memory usage, although Levenshtein distance only requires the previous row to calculate the next row.

### Proposed change

Replace the full matrix implementation with a rolling array implementation:

- Keep the same Levenshtein distance behavior.
- Reduce memory usage from `O(n*m)` to `O(min(n,m))`.
- Reduce temporary heap allocations during command suggestion generation.

### Benchmark

Benchmarking the current implementation against a rolling-array implementation:

```bash

title: PowerShell autocompletion script fails with runtime errors on empty or single-item completions
body:
### Description
Cobra's generated PowerShell completion script fails with runtime exceptions in various edge cases due to how it parses and filters the completion output array (`$Out`):

1. **Null Pointer/MethodNotFound Exceptions on Empty Outputs:**
   If a command execution returns no output (for example, if the CLI binary crashes, fails or simply yields no completions and stdout is empty), the array `$Out` is empty. The generated script calls `$Out[-1].TrimStart(':')` without checking if `$Out` contains any elements. This throws a fatal PowerShell error:
   ```text
   You cannot call a method on a null-valued expression.
   ```

2. **System.Char vs. String Type Confusion:**
   PowerShell pipelines automatically unwrap arrays containing exactly one element into a scalar object (such as `System.String`). In the next execution phase, querying `$Out[-1]` returns a `System.Char` instead of a `System.String`. Since `System.Char` does not have a `TrimStart` method, calling it throws:
   ```text
   Method invocation failed because [System.Char] does not contain a method named 'TrimStart'.
   ```

3. **Filtering Collision on Identical String Values:**
   To strip the directive (which is the last element of the output, such as `:4`), the script uses:
   ```powershell
   $Out = $Out | Where-Object { $_ -ne $Out[-1] }
   ```
   Instead of removing only the last item by index, this filters out all items matching the value of the last item. If a command legitimately outputs a completion item that matches the directive string (such as when a flag or argument completes to the string `":0"`), it is incorrectly stripped.

### Root Cause Analysis
In `powershell_completions.go` inside the shell script template, the generated script assumes `$Out` is always a populated array with string elements:

```powershell
    #call the command store the output in $out and redirect stderr and stdout to null
    Invoke-Expression -OutVariable out "$RequestComp" 2>&1 | Out-Null

    # get directive from last line
    [int]$Directive = $Out[-1].TrimStart(':')
    if ($Directive -eq "") {
        $Directive = 0
    }

    # remove directive (last element) from out
    $Out = $Out | Where-Object { $_ -ne $Out[-1] }
```

### Proposed Fix
Modify the template inside `powershell_completions.go` to safely check the size of the array, convert the directive to an integer defensively and strip the last item cleanly by index using `Select-Object`:

```go
	$Directive = 0
	if ($Out.Count -gt 0) {
		$DirectiveStr = $Out[-1].TrimStart(':')
		if ($DirectiveStr -ne "") {
			$Directive = [int]$DirectiveStr
		}
		$Out = $Out | Select-Object -First ($Out.Count - 1)
	}
	__%[1]s_debug "The completion directive is: $Directive"
	__%[1]s_debug "The completions are: $Out"
```
evidence: PowerShell autocompletion script fails with runtime errors on empty or single-item completions

**Null Pointer/MethodNotFound Exceptions on Empty Outputs:** If a command execution returns no output (for example, if the CLI binary crashes, fails or simply yields no completions and stdout is empty), the array `$Out` is empty.

title: label_replace: a NULLABLE capture group sharing a name is still an unexpressible divergence
body:
Successor to #1768. Tracks the residue of one divergence: a capture-group NAME
several groups share, where which group `$name` expands to turns on **which
group took part in the match** rather than on what any group captured.

## The gap

Go's `Regexp.expand` resolves `$name` by scanning `SubexpNames()` for the first
index `i` with `match[2*i] >= 0` — the first carrier that **took part**.
ClickHouse's `extractGroups` renders "did not take part" and "took part, matched
empty" identically, both as `''`, so participation is not directly observable
from SQL.

Upstream: **ClickHouse/ClickHouse#114733**. re2 carries the bit —
a non-participating group comes back with `data() == nullptr` — and
`src/Functions/extractGroups.cpp` discards it by calling `insertData(...)`
unconditionally into a hard-coded `Array(String)`. If that function grows a
nullable-returning form, this whole class collapses and the guard here can be
deleted rather than narrowed.

## Current boundary

The guard has been narrowed twice, each time against an exhaustive corpus with
an exact differential against Go's `ExpandString`.

- **#2116** narrowed it from "any nullable carrier" to real participation
  ambiguity, using three positional facts: a non-nullable carrier can never be
  the culprit; a carrier every match passes through truncates the search; and
  two carriers in different branches of one alternation never co-occur.
- **#2124** narrowed it again by rewriting the regex rather than reasoning about
  it — see the comment below for the mechanism and the measurements.

What is rejected today is a carrier that a match can skip, that co-occurs with a
later carrier which can capture text, **and** that has no span above it which
both cannot match empty and is passed through on every match. Concretely: a
carrier alone in a nullable alternation branch, or alone under a quest.

```promql
label_replace(up, "d", "$dup", "src", "(?:(?P<dup>a?)|y)(?P<dup>b)")
```

On `src="b"` Prometheus answers `d=""` — the empty branch took part — while the
emitted search answers `d="b"`.

## Where it is pinned

- `test/rejection-parity/catalogue/internal__promql__label_fns.go.json` —
  `lowerLabelReplace#d11e3df4`
- `test/rejection-parity/catalogue/internal__logql__label_fns.go.json` —
  `lowerLabelReplace#8cd9f67b`

Both carry the trigger query above and must cite this issue while it stays open.
The head-side boundary is pinned on both sides by
`TestLowerLabelReplace_RejectsInexpressibleBackref` and
`TestLowerLabelReplace_AcceptsSharedCaptureName` in each head.

## Done when

Either the two remaining cerberus-side mechanisms below are built and the guard
narrows to nothing, or ClickHouse/ClickHouse#114733 lands and the guard is
deleted outright. At that point both catalogue entries drop their `divergence`
classification and the two head tests flip to their acceptance twin.

labels.name: upstream
labels.description: Blocked on an upstream dependency's own fix; tracked here until it lands

comments:
Investigated end to end; PR #2116 lands the outcome. Two findings, and the second changes the shape of this issue:

1. ClickHouse still cannot report capture-group participation, on any version cerberus can target.
2. **Participation was never the only way to settle the question, and the guard was over-broad.** The
   trigger query this issue was filed with — `(?P<dup>a?)|(?P<dup>b)` — is expressible, and now
   lowers and answers.

The residue is real, so this stays open, but it is much narrower than "any nullable carrier" and is
now characterised exactly.

## 1. No ClickHouse construction exposes participation

Investigated against the substrate cerberus actually runs: **ClickHouse 26.6** (`docker-compose.yml`),
with the compat lanes on 26.5 and the supported floor at 24.8.

The near miss is **`regexpPosition`** (aliases `regexp_instr` / `regexpInstr`), which did not exist
when this issue was filed — it landed in **26.5** (ClickHouse/ClickHouse#104172). Its 7th argument
selects a *capture group*, so it looks exactly like the missing primitive:

```
regexpPosition(haystack, pattern[, position[, occurrence[, return_option[, flags[, subexpression]]]]]) -> UInt64
```

It does not work, and the docs are misleading about why. They say it "Returns 0 if no match is found,
or if the requested capture group did not participate in the match" — but it *also* returns 0 for a
group that participated and matched the empty string. Verified empirically on chDB 26.5.1.1:

```sql
-- group 2 never participates; group 3 participates matching empty at offset 1.
SELECT extractGroups('ab', '^(a)(x)?(b?)(b)$');               -- ['a','','','b']
SELECT regexpPosition('ab', '^(a)(x)?(b?)(b)$', 1,1,0,'', 2); -- 0  (did not participate)
SELECT regexpPosition('ab', '^(a)(x)?(b?)(b)$', 1,1,0,'', 3); -- 0  (participated, empty)  <-- same
SELECT regexpPosition('ab', '^(a)(x)?(b?)(b)$', 1,1,0,'', 4); -- 2
```

The cause is one layer below the function: `OptimizedRegularExpression::match`
(`src/Common/OptimizedRegularExpression.cpp`) tests each re2 submatch with
`std::string_view::empty()`, which is `size() == 0`, and folds a participating zero-length capture
onto the same `npos` sentinel as a non-participating one. Every caller on that path inherits the
loss, so no position- or offset-based workaround can recover the bit either. (`0` is additionally the
return for "the pattern did not match at all", and reading N groups costs N regex executions.)

Everything else on the surface was checked and is uninformative for this question: `match`,
`extract`, `extractGroups`, `extractAllGroups{Horizontal,Vertical}`, `replaceRegexpOne` /
`replaceRegexpAll`, `regexpExtract`, `countMatches`, `splitByRegexp`, and the `multiMatch*` family.
None reports per-group participation, and none returns `Nullable` per group.

Worth recording for whoever revisits this: in `src/Functions/extractGroups.cpp` the bit is still
*intact* at the point it is thrown away. That function calls re2 directly, and re2 documents that a
non-participating group comes back with `data() == nullptr`; extractGroups then does
`insertData(matched_groups[group].data(), matched_groups[group].size())`, appending an empty string
either way, into a return type hard-coded to `Array(String)`. So an upstream fix confined to
`extractGroups` — returning `Array(Nullable(String))` — is local and cheap, and would collapse this
whole issue. No such ClickHouse issue or feature request exists today (four search strategies over
`ClickHouse/ClickHouse` surfaced none).

## 2. The guard was over-broad — #1952's condition is sufficient, not necessary

Go's `Regexp.expand` resolves `$name` to the first carrier that TOOK PART in the match; the emitted
SQL resolves it to the first carrier whose capture is NON-EMPTY. Enumerating when those two searches
can differ turns out to be the whole problem, and the answer is a single event:

> the first carrier to take part captures the **empty string**, **and** a later carrier **in that same
> match** captures text.

Every other combination agrees — including the case that looks dangerous, "the first participant
captured empty and every later carrier is empty too", where both searches yield `''`.

Non-nullability rules that event out, which is what #1952 shipped. But two other facts, both readable
straight off `regexp/syntax`'s parse tree, rule it out just as soundly:

**(a) Truncate at the first carrier every match must pass through.** Go's scan can never walk past a
carrier that always participates, so every carrier after it is unreachable and its nullability is
irrelevant. `(?P<dup>a?)(?P<dup>b)` collapses to "group 1", full stop.

**(b) Mutual exclusion.** Two carriers in different branches of one alternation never take part in the
same match, so an empty capture by the earlier one implies the later one did not participate and
reads as `''` as well. (Unless a repetition *around* the alternation re-enters it — `(?:x(?P<dup>a?)|(?P<dup>b))*`
on `bbbx` really does reach both, so that arm stays rejected.)

A corollary falls out of the same analysis: **the last carrier's nullability never matters**, because
the failure mode needs a later carrier to skip ahead to.

(b) is exactly this issue's trigger query. `(?P<dup>a?)|(?P<dup>b)`: on `""` carrier 1 takes part
capturing nothing and carrier 2 is `''`, so both searches answer `""`; on `"b"` carrier 1 never took
part and both answer `"b"`.

### Measured

Exhaustive corpus of 33 structural arrangements (23 two-carrier, 10 three-carrier) crossed with every
combination of 9 carrier subpatterns = **9153 regexes**, each checked against `ExpandString` on every
input string over `{a,b,x,y}` of length ≤ 3:

| | accepted | share |
|---|---|---|
| old guard (no carrier may be nullable) | 1008 | 11.0% |
| new guard | **5598** | **61.2%** |

Zero disagreements with `ExpandString` among the accepted set. Independently re-derived and fuzzed
from a clean-room reimplementation during review — 268k regexes across hand-built three-carrier
templates, non-greedy / `\b` / `(?i)` / factorable-prefix shapes, and a random-grammar generator —
also zero.

The corpus and both directions of the check are now checked in as
`TestExpressibleCarriersAgreeWithExpandString` and `TestExpressibleCarriersRejectionsHaveWitnesses`
in `internal/qlcommon/capture_participation_test.go`. The second one holds the *rejected* set
accountable too, so a future guard cannot quietly drift back towards over-rejecting; and the
three-carrier arrangements are load-bearing rather than decorative, because with only two carriers
the "exclusive of EVERY later carrier" test can never inspect more than one element — a mutant
checking only the next carrier passed a two-carrier corpus with an identical accept count.

## 3. What is still inexpressible

A nullable carrier a match can **skip**, while a later carrier that **can co-occur** with it captures
text. Smallest witness:

```promql
label_replace(up, "d", "$dup", "src", "(?:x(?P<dup>a?))?(?P<dup>b)")
```

On `src="xb"` the optional branch takes part and `dup` captures nothing, so Prometheus answers
`d=""`, while a first-non-empty search answers `d="b"`. Both catalogue entries now pin this query
instead of the old one, and both head tests pin it as the rejection boundary.

## 4. The construction that would close the rest (identified, not built)

Participation of a nullable carrier *is* recoverable without any new ClickHouse function, by changing
the regex rather than the expression: walk up from the carrier to the nearest ancestor whose subtree
is **non-nullable** and which no optional node separates from the carrier, and wrap that ancestor in a
fresh capture group. That probe group participates exactly when the carrier does, and — being
non-nullable — is non-empty exactly when it participates. `(?:x(?P<dup>a?))?(?P<dup>b)` becomes
`(?:((?:x(?P<dup>a?))))?(?P<dup>b)`, and the probe's emptiness is the carrier's participation bit.
The selection then emits as `multiIf(p1, g1, p2, g2, …, '')` rather than `arrayFirst`.

Not built here, for reasons worth recording:

- it requires reconstructing a regex **string** from a mutated `syntax.Regexp` tree, and
  `Regexp.String()` round-tripping is not something to bet a user-supplied regex's semantics on;
- it needs new `chplan` IR (a per-carrier probe index) and a new emitter shape, so it is a second
  change of comparable size to this one, not an increment on it;
- it still would not close everything: `(?:(?P<dup>a?)|y)(?P<dup>b)` has no non-nullable ancestor to
  probe, and would need the inverse trick — probing the *sibling* branch and reading participation
  negatively.

## 5. Re-check trigger

Re-open this analysis if ClickHouse ever returns `Array(Nullable(String))` from `extractGroups`, or
adds any function reporting per-group match offsets. Either one collapses the whole problem to a
`isNull(...)` test and the guard disappears entirely.

Reopened. PR #2116 merged and GitHub auto-closed this issue, which was not intended — the PR body carried the sentence "This does **not** close #1956", and GitHub's closing-keyword parser matches `close #1956` regardless of the negation in front of it. The PR body has been reworded so the keyword is gone.

The residue described above stands and is still open work: a nullable carrier a match can SKIP while a later carrier that can co-occur with it captures text, e.g. `(?:x(?P<dup>a?))?(?P<dup>b)`. Both rejection-parity catalogue entries and both head tests pin that query, and `test/rejection-parity/divergence-ceiling.json` still allows the same 3 divergence entries it did before.

## Probe-group rewrite — shipped in #2124

Participation turns out to be recoverable by changing the **regex** rather than
the expression. Walk up from the carrier to the nearest span that (a) cannot
match the empty string and (b) every match of which passes through the carrier,
and wrap that span in a synthetic capture group. It takes part exactly when the
carrier does, and being non-nullable it is non-empty exactly when it takes part
— so its emptiness *is* the participation bit.

```
(?:x(?P<dup>a?))?(?P<dup>b)
(?:(?P<cerberusprobe0>x(?P<dup>a?)))?(?P<dup>b)
```

Emitted as `arrayFirst((x, p) -> p != '', [values], [probes])` over the
rewritten pattern — predicate reads the participation array, answer comes from
the value array.

This answers the objection the old body raised ("making the carrier's
subpattern non-nullable changes which inputs the overall regex matches"): the
carrier's subpattern is untouched, and the added group only observes. Language
preservation is checked span by span on every rewritten regex, not argued.

Spans are located by scanning the regex **source**, because `regexp/syntax`
records no byte offsets — but every judgement about a span is made by handing
the substring back to `regexp/syntax`, so the parse tree stays the authority on
meaning and the scanner only answers "which bytes".

### Measured

Exhaustive corpus, extended with the literal-bearing alternation shapes the
rewrite turns on. 11907 regexes: **6912 accepted before, 8417 after** (58.0% →
70.7%), every one agreeing with Go's `ExpandString` on every input, exactly.

### One hazard found

A bare inline `(?flags)` setting applies to the end of its enclosing group,
**crossing alternation branches**. Wrapping one branch confines it, so
`(?:(?i)a|b)` matches `"B"` before a rewrite and not after — a real language
change. Patterns carrying one are never rewritten, and the hazard is pinned as a
running test. The scoped `(?flags:…)` spelling carries its setting with it and
stays allowed.

## What is left, and what would close it

The remaining 3490 corpus regexes split into two further mechanisms, both
verified as real rather than guessed:

**1. Negative sibling probe.** A carrier alone in a nullable alternation branch
has nothing to probe, but its *siblings* do. If every other branch is
non-nullable, probe each of them; the carrier took part exactly when the
alternation was entered and no sibling probe fired. Needs the alternation to be
entered at most once per match (no re-enterable ancestor) and its entry to be
observable. Measured on the 9153-regex corpus as it stood before this round's
extension: **835 of the 3085 then-rejected regexes (27.1%)** become expressible.
Not built here — it turns the emitted form from a two-array `arrayFirst` into a
general `multiIf` with conjunctive predicates, which is a comparable second
change.

**2. Greedy empty-path participation.** The residue after (1) is shapes like
`(?:(?P<dup>a?))?(?P<dup>b)`, where the optional group is *always* entered under
greedy matching — entering and matching empty always succeeds and is preferred
— so the carrier is effectively unconditional. Deciding this means computing,
for a nullable subtree, which capture groups take part on its **preferred empty
match**, following RE2's leftmost-first preference order. Decidable and not
large, but it is a genuinely different analysis from the positional facts the
current guard uses, and it is sensitive to non-greedy quantifiers and the `U`
flag.

Neither is blocked. Both are strictly smaller in value than
ClickHouse/ClickHouse#114733 landing, which would let all of this be deleted
rather than extended — so the honest ordering is to wait on upstream first and
build (1) and (2) only if that stalls.

body:
## Found by

The first-ever full-depth (`SWEEP_DEPTH=full`) crawl of the k3d stack
(`CRAWL_STACK=k3d`), run to bootstrap `grafana-surface-inventory.k3d.json`
in #1539.

## Evidence

Two oracle violations trace to the same root cause — the Traces Drilldown
app's `var-primarySignal` set to the attribute-based filter
`span.db.system.name!=""`:

**`console-error`** on
`/a/grafana-exploretraces-app/explore?var-metric=duration&var-primarySignal=span.db.system.name!=""`:

```
runRequest.catchError Error: rpc error: code = InvalidArgument desc = traceql parse stage:
parse error at line 1, col 47: syntax error: unexpected }, expecting an attribute
```

**`panel-no-data-undeclared`** (the downstream symptom — the query above
never returns data, so a panel renders empty) on
`/a/grafana-exploretraces-app/explore?var-primarySignal=span.db.system.name!=""#radio[Single|Grid|Rows]=Single`:

```
panel "<untitled panel>" rendered "No data" with no cerberus.expect declaration
(url=/a/grafana-exploretraces-app/explore?...&var-primarySignal=span.db.system.name%21%3D%22%22&
var-filters=&var-metric=rate&var-groupBy=resource.service.name&...)
```

`span.db.system.name!=""` is one of the k3d stack's seeded/enumerated
`var-primarySignal` values (see `enumerating var-primarySignal keeps every
signal a distinct surface` in `crawl/crawl.spec.ts`, and #1873/#1872's
work on primarySignal enumeration). The value is a raw TraceQL attribute
comparison fragment, and something in the query-template substitution path
(Traces Drilldown's query builder, or cerberus's TraceQL surface) isn't
producing valid TraceQL when this specific fragment is interpolated — "col
47: unexpected }, expecting an attribute" points at a brace/quote
imbalance in the generated query, not a cerberus-side rejection of
otherwise-valid TraceQL.

Against a healthy k3d stack (`just e2e-up && just e2e-seed-rolling`), open
`/a/grafana-exploretraces-app/explore` with `var-primarySignal=span.db.system.name!=""`
and `var-metric=duration` (or `rate`) set. The query issued to cerberus's
Tempo-compatible endpoint fails to parse.

## Scope note

Not fixed here — found while bootstrapping the k3d crawl inventory (#1539).
This is a real, deterministic parse failure (not timing-sensitive); whether
it also reproduces on the compose stack depends on whether that stack's
primarySignal enumeration includes the same `span.db.system.name!=""`
attribute value.

comments:
Confirmed reproducing on the **compose** stack too, from the first-ever clean (non-masked) full-depth compose crawl — resolving the open question in this issue's own "Scope note."

Same two violations, byte-identical evidence:
- `console-error` on `/a/grafana-exploretraces-app/explore?var-metric=duration&var-primarySignal=span.db.system.name!=""`: `traceql parse stage: parse error at line 1, col 47: syntax error: unexpected }, expecting an attribute`
- `panel-no-data-undeclared` on the same `var-primarySignal` value with `var-metric=rate`.

Context: found while running PR #2020's (#1872) sanctioned dispatch-driven full-depth regen, on the first run whose real output wasn't masked by the retry/timeout bug fixed in that PR's own `32e1397a`. Confirms this is a real, deterministic, cross-stack bug — not k3d-specific.

## Root-caused with the wire query captured — two independent causes, neither a cerberus parser bug

I captured the literal TraceQL text cerberus receives, which no previous pass had. It never appears in HTTP traffic: the Tempo datasource is provisioned with streaming search (`test/e2e/grafana/compose/datasources/cerberus.yaml`), so the query travels over Grafana Live (`ws://localhost:3000/api/live/ws`) into cerberus's h2c gRPC `StreamingQuerier` on :8080. That is why the message carries a `rpc error: code = InvalidArgument` prefix, and why replaying the `/api/ds/query` POST bodies never reproduced it — every one of those parses and returns 200.

Captured WebSocket subscribe frame (compose stack, Grafana 12.2.9, `grafana-exploretraces-app` 2.1.0):

```json
{"subscribe":{"channel":"1/ds/cerberus-tempo/search/135ea56e-67bd-4f77-b14e-405b6973aef6",
 "data":{"refId":"A","query":"{span.db.system.name!=\"\" && true&& duration > }",
 "queryType":"traceql","tableType":"spans","limit":200,"spss":10,"filters":[]}},"id":2}
```

**The query text is:**

```
{span.db.system.name!="" && true&& duration > }
```

That string is 47 characters and column 47 is the closing `}`. `duration >` has no right-hand operand. Cerberus's error names the position exactly right; replayed straight at the HTTP head:

```console
$ curl -sG http://localhost:8080/api/search --data-urlencode 'q={span.db.system.name!="" && true&& duration > }'
HTTP 400
{"error":true,"message":"traceql parse stage: parse error at line 1, col 47: syntax error: unexpected }, expecting an attribute"}
```

**Cerberus is correct to reject this.** There is nothing to fix in `internal/traceql`.

---

### Cause 1 (the `console-error`) — upstream plugin bug, and NOT specific to this primary signal

The malformed text is built by the plugin's own query builder. Upstream is **`grafana/traces-drilldown`** (renamed from `grafana/explore-traces`; the plugin id is still `grafana-exploretraces-app`). Plugin 2.1.0 = tag `v2.1.0` = `932bac31b336045371c26739192e3f8967d1606a`.

`src/components/Explore/TracesByService/TracesByServiceScene.tsx`, `buildQuery`, **line 425**:

```ts
if (!typeQuery.length) {
  typeQuery = `&& duration > ${VAR_LATENCY_THRESHOLD_EXPR}`;   // line 425
}
...
return {
  refId: 'A',
  query: `{${VAR_FILTERS_EXPR}${typeQuery}}${selectQuery}`,     // line 431
  ...
};
```

with `VAR_FILTERS_EXPR = '${primarySignal} && ${filters}'` and `VAR_LATENCY_THRESHOLD_EXPR = '${latencyThreshold}'` (`src/utils/shared.ts:35,41`).

`latencyThreshold` is declared **with no initial value** (`src/pages/Explore/TraceExploration.tsx:529-540`) and is assigned only from inside the RED duration-histogram data subscriber (`src/components/Explore/TracesByService/REDPanel.tsx:112-119`). `buildQuery` has no dependency on that, so the span-list query fires before the histogram has returned and `${latencyThreshold}` interpolates to the empty string. The missing space before `&&` is the same template's fingerprint: the `errors` arm uses `' && status = error'` (leading space), the `duration` arm uses `'&& …'`.

Present continuously since commit `8b3906f3` (2024-09-05) and **byte-identical on `main` today** — not fixed. The repo's own unit test pins the malformed shape at `TracesByServiceScene.test.tsx:67`.

**This is an init-race that fires on every primary signal, not just the database one.** I drove all five enumerated values; each emits the dangling query first, then recovers once the histogram resolves the threshold:

| `var-primarySignal` | queries sent, in order | recovers? |
|---|---|---|
| `nestedSetParent<0` (default) | `{nestedSetParent<0 && true&& duration > }` → `… > 134ms` → `… >= 134ms` | yes |
| `true` | `{true && true&& duration > }` → `… > 67ms` → `… >= 67ms` | yes |
| `kind=server` | `{kind=server && true&& duration > }` → `… > 134ms` → `… >= 134ms` | yes |
| `kind=consumer` | `{kind=consumer && true&& duration > }` → `… > 0` → `… >= 0` | yes |
| `span.db.system.name!=""` | `{span.db.system.name!="" && true&& duration > }` | **never** |

So the issue title's attribution to `span.db.system.name!=""` should be widened: **every** Traces Drilldown page load emits one guaranteed 400. The database signal is only special in that it never recovers — see Cause 2.

This is the same class the harness already knows about: `iterate-drilldown-apps.spec.ts:353-370` documents two dangling-operand shapes (`{ && …}`, the primarySignal race; `{… && undefined != nil} … by(undefined)`, the groupBy race) and `isTransientMalformedTraceQLFailure` reconciles them. **The latency-threshold shape `{… && duration > }` is a third variant that reconciler does not recognise** — which is exactly why the crawl's console-error oracle fires here while `iterate-drilldown-apps` stays green.

Upstream siblings of the same class (unguarded interpolation of an unresolved Scenes variable into a TraceQL string): [grafana/traces-drilldown#765](https://github.com/grafana/traces-drilldown/issues/765) (open, zero comments, `by(undefined)`), [#95](https://github.com/grafana/traces-drilldown/issues/95) (closed 2024-12-20 with no guard in the referenced diff). A precedent fix for the same shape already exists in that repo at `src/components/Explore/queries/generateMetricsQuery.ts:36-57`, which guards the resolved value before emitting the fragment that consumes it.

### Cause 2 (the `panel-no-data-undeclared`) — an OTel semconv mismatch in our own seed, not a downstream symptom

The issue assumed one root cause ("the query above never returns data, so a panel renders empty"). That is not what happens — the metric queries return HTTP 200 and parse fine. The panel is empty because **the seed contains no spans carrying `db.system.name`**:

```
{span.db.system.name!=""} | rate()  ->  1 series, sum(values) = 0
{span.db.system!=""}      | rate()  ->  1 series, sum(values) = 1.3167
{kind=server}             | rate()  ->  1 series, sum(values) = 0.7333
```

`test/e2e/seed/cmd/seed/main.go:502,504` and `showcase_traceql.go:79,108` emit `map('db.system', 'postgres'|'redis')` — the pre-1.21 OTel semantic convention. Cerberus's `/api/v2/search/tags` confirms the span scope advertises `db.system`, with no `db.system.name`. The plugin's built-in "Database calls" signal filters `span.db.system.name`, the ≥1.21 stabilized name. **Zero matches is the correct answer from cerberus.**

This also explains the asymmetry in the table above: because nothing matches, the RED histogram returns empty, `REDPanel`'s subscriber never runs, `latencyThreshold` never resolves, and this signal alone never re-fires a valid query.

Worth noting before anyone "fixes" the seed: `internal/chclient/client.go:29` states cerberus deliberately uses "v1.0-vintage `db.system` / `db.statement` keys" for its own self-instrumentation, and `internal/chclient/execute_span_test.go:77` pins it. So aligning the seed to `db.system.name` is a deliberate convention decision, not a typo fix — flagging rather than unilaterally changing it.

### Recommendation

1. **Cause 1 → report upstream** at `grafana/traces-drilldown`, as the third instance of one class, linking #765 rather than filing a standalone bug. The minimal fix is either to give `VAR_LATENCY_THRESHOLD` an initial value at `TraceExploration.tsx:531`, or to read the resolved value and skip the clause when unset, mirroring `generateMetricsQuery.ts:36-57`. Any fix must update `TracesByServiceScene.test.tsx:67`, which currently asserts the malformed string.
2. **Cause 2 → ours to decide**: either seed `db.system.name` so the "Database calls" signal exercises a real query path, or accept the empty panel as correct and declare it. The former is better coverage; the latter is a suppression.
3. Cerberus's parser and error message are correct in both cases. The one cosmetic nit: for `duration > }` the message says "expecting an attribute", though a static (`500ms`) would be equally valid there — "expecting an attribute or a static" would read truer. Not worth a change on its own.

### Reproduction

Wire capture used a headless Chromium against the running compose stack with `page.on('websocket')` frame capture — the HTTP-only captures in the earlier passes are what hid the query text. Verified on compose (Grafana 12.2.9, plugin 2.1.0); the k3d evidence in the issue body is byte-identical.

Filed upstream: grafana/traces-drilldown#850 (unguarded `latencyThreshold` interpolation, extending the same class as their #765/#95). Full evidence in the comment above. Cause 2 (the panel-no-data OTel semconv mismatch) remains ours to decide — see the recommendation in that comment; this issue stays open to track both.

title: traceql: duration > span.<dynamic-int-attribute> answers where reference Tempo returns zero
body:
## The divergence

`{ duration > span.child.index }` — comparing the `duration` intrinsic against a dynamic (per-span, not statically typed) attribute whose actual per-row values are Int — is a live behavioral divergence between cerberus and reference Tempo, not a static-typing question (both correctly ACCEPT the query; `TypeAttribute` matches any operand per `isMatchingOperand` in `internal/traceql/ast/validate.go`, since a dynamic attribute's real type isn't known until row-evaluation).

Discovered while working PR #2034 (#2033): the fix there repointed a previously empty-vs-empty compat case (`duration_gt_dynamic_attribute` in `compatibility/tempo/driver/corpus/smoke.txtar`) at a real numeric attribute (`span.child.index`, written on every child span by the seeder) to make it a genuine non-empty-vs-non-empty comparison. Against the real compat harness:

- reference Tempo: **0 traces** for `{ duration > span.child.index }`
- cerberus: **100 traces**

Reverted that repoint back to the original `span.budget_ns` (an attribute the seeder never writes, so both backends agree on an empty answer) rather than block #2034 on this — that PR's subject is static type-checking, not per-row dynamic-attribute coercion, and this deserves its own investigation.

## Working hypothesis

Reference Tempo's per-row comparison evaluator likely requires the attribute's *actual* per-row value to be duration-typed (or otherwise directly comparable) for a `duration >` comparison to match anything — an Int-typed attribute value like `child.index` never satisfies that, so every span fails the filter and the trace-level answer is correctly empty on every trace. Cerberus's lowering (`internal/traceql/lower.go`'s `binaryHasNumericOperand`/`coerceNumericFieldAccess` family, or wherever the dynamic-attribute side of a duration comparison is coerced) appears to coerce any numeric-looking attribute value into a comparable form regardless of its OTel/TraceQL type, which is more permissive than the reference and produces false matches.

Not yet root-caused at the exact `internal/traceql`/`internal/chsql` line — this issue is the tracking home for whoever picks it up next.

## To close this

Root-cause the coercion cerberus applies to a dynamic-attribute operand in a `duration >`/`<`/`>=`/`<=` comparison, and either:
- narrow it to only match when the attribute's per-row OTel value type is genuinely duration-compatible (matching Tempo), or
- if cerberus's broader coercion is an intentional divergence (answering more than Tempo does), document that decision explicitly and adjust the compat baseline with a real justification — never by silently accepting the mismatch into the baseline as agreement.

Re-point `compatibility/tempo/driver/corpus/smoke.txtar`'s `duration_gt_dynamic_attribute` case at `span.child.index` (or another real numeric attribute) once the lowering is fixed, so this case actually exercises non-empty data on both sides again — the empty-vs-empty form it's reverted to can't tell a correct lowering from a broken one that also happens to drop all rows.

title: promql: exp-histogram binop matching modifiers + ==/!= still unsupported after #2263
body:
## What's still missing after #2263

#2263 adds `+`/`-` between two exponential-histogram (native-histogram) selectors with *default* vector matching only. Two related shapes reference Prometheus also answers are deliberately left out of that change, to keep its blast radius proportionate to the issue's own ask:

### 1. `on()`/`ignoring()`/`group_left()`/`group_right()` matching for `+`/`-` between two histograms

Reference Prometheus's vector-matching machinery (which resolves *which* pairs of series combine) is orthogonal to `vectorElemBinop`'s per-pair histogram arithmetic — `demo_latency_exp_hist + on(job) demo_other_exp_hist` is valid upstream and merges the matched pair's distributions exactly like the default-matching case.

Cerberus's new `internal/promql/histogram_native_binop.go` explicitly rejects any non-default `VectorMatching` with a dedicated error ("on()/ignoring()/group_left()/group_right() matching is not yet supported for binary arithmetic between two exponential histogram selectors"), because its merge is built as a `UnionAll` + `Aggregate` grouped by the full `Attributes` map with a `count() = 2` `Having` guard standing in for `VectorJoin`'s default one-to-one INNER JOIN — extending that to an arbitrary match-key subset (and to `group_left`/`group_right`'s many-to-one broadcast) needs either generalizing `chplan.VectorJoin` to carry multiple histogram payload columns per side, or a dedicated histogram-aware join node mirroring `VectorJoin`'s existing per-side aggregation + uniqueness-guard machinery (`internal/chsql/vector_join.go`).

The rejection-parity catalogue entry `internal/promql/lower.go:expHistogramSelectorRouting#bf746b59` now cites this issue as its `divergence` tracking issue, with `trigger_query: "demo_latency_exp_hist + demo_latency_exp_hist on(job)"` (reference accepts, cerberus rejects).

### 2. `==`/`!=` between two histograms

Reference Prometheus's `vectorElemBinop` (`promql/engine.go`) answers `hist1 == hist2` / `hist1 != hist2` with a *structural-equality filter*, not a merge: `hlhs.Equals(hrhs)` decides whether the pair is kept, and the kept row's value is the LHS histogram unchanged. This is different machinery from the bucket-merge `+`/`-` reuse (`expHistogramMergeAggs`/`Projections`) — it needs a Scale/ZeroCount/ZeroThreshold/bucket-array structural-equality expression (not a reconciled-scale sum), and reference's own doc notes both histograms must already be compacted for the comparison to be meaningful.

`*`, `/`, `^`, `%`, `atan2`, and every other comparison between two histograms are NOT supported by reference Prometheus either (`NewIncompatibleTypesInBinOpInfo`) — cerberus's existing rejection at `expHistogramSelectorRouting` already matches that, no gap there.

### Why filed now rather than folded into #2263

Both are genuinely separate mechanisms from the bucket-merge #2263 ships (a different join/matching shape for #1, a different per-pair operation for #2), each with its own design/implementation cost. Filing them here keeps them visible instead of letting the finding evaporate the moment #2263 merges.
comments:
## Refined implementation shape for gap 1 (matching modifiers)

Investigated this concretely (didn't ship it this session — see below). Splitting the gap by cardinality
changes the picture from how this issue currently frames it:

### `on()`/`ignoring()` with default (one-to-one) cardinality — tractable without touching `chplan.VectorJoin`

The existing `+`/`-` and `==`/`!=` lowerings (`histogram_native_binop.go`, `histogram_native_binop_eq.go`)
do **not** use `chplan.VectorJoin` at all — they use `UnionAll` + `Aggregate` grouped by the full
`Attributes` map, with `histogramBinopBothSidesMatchedGuard` (`count() = 2`) standing in for the INNER
JOIN. The bucket-merge fold itself (`expHistogramMergeBucketsBoundsExpr` /
`expHistogramMergeOffsetExpr` / `expHistogramRowContribsExpr`, shared verbatim with the cross-series
`sum()` merge) is **already N-ary and array-based** — it folds over however many rows `groupArray`
collected, not specifically two. `count() = 2` is the only place cardinality "2" is hard-coded.

That means matching on a label subset doesn't need a join — it needs the same UnionAll+Aggregate shape,
regrouped:

1. **Group-by key**: swap the full-`Attributes` key for a reduced key. `ignoring(labels)` already has a
   reusable chplan primitive — `chplan.MapWithoutKeys` (used today by `sum without(...)` in
   `histogramAggGroupBy`, `internal/promql/histogram_quantile.go`). `on(labels)` has no equivalent yet — a
   small new `MapOnlyKeys`-shaped chplan node (mirroring `MapWithoutKeys`'s doc/Equal/clone/emitter
   plumbing, `mapFilter((k,v) -> k IN (...), Attributes)`) closes that gap. Both are Map-valued
   expressions, no new Aggregate machinery.
2. **One-to-one uniqueness guard**: `count() = 2` only works because grouping by the *full* Attributes map
   already guarantees at most one row per side per group. Reduced to a label subset, a group can now
   collect more than one row from the *same* side (genuine many-to-many), so `count() = 2` must become a
   **per-side** count check. The `==`/`!=` lowering already has the side-discriminator machinery this
   needs: `histEqSideAlias` + `chplan.AggCombinator.CombIf`-qualified `groupArrayIf`. The guard generalizes
   to `countIf(side=L) = 1 AND countIf(side=R) = 1` (built the same way, `Fn: chplan.FnCount,
   Combinators: [chplan.CombIf], Args: [sideCond]` — no new chplan Fn needed). `+`/`-` doesn't tag sides
   today (its `count()=2` doesn't need to); adding the same `histEqSideAlias` tagging is a small extension,
   not new machinery.
3. **Output Attributes**: reference's `resultMetric` Keep/Del reduction for `CardOneToOne` (the same rule
   `internal/chsql/vector_join.go`'s `outputMatchSetFrag` already implements for the *scalar* V-V path) —
   for the histogram path the reduced group-by key IS the output Attributes directly, no separate
   rebuild step needed beyond what already exists.

None of this touches `chplan.VectorJoin` / `internal/chsql/vector_join.go`, so the well-tested scalar V-V
path carries zero risk from this change. It would apply uniformly to `+`, `-`, `==`, `!=`.

### `group_left()`/`group_right()` (many-to-one broadcast) — genuinely needs join machinery

This is where the UnionAll+Aggregate approach breaks down, confirming this issue's original framing for
*this* card only: the "many" side must keep per-series granularity in the output while the "one" side's
single matched value gets broadcast onto every one of the many side's rows. A `GROUP BY <reduced key>`
necessarily collapses both sides onto the match key — there's no way to preserve the many side's own
per-series identity in the output *and* still get a single grouped row per match key. This needs either:

- generalizing `chplan.VectorJoin` to carry a variable/multi-column payload per side (touches the
  well-tested scalar V-V join emitter — `internal/chsql/vector_join.go`'s per-side `argMax`/`roleMany`/
  `roleOne` aggregation, `outputAttributesFrag`'s mapConcat broadcast, etc., all built around exactly one
  `ValueColumn`), or
- a dedicated histogram-payload join node that mirrors that machinery (`vectorJoinRoles`,
  `matchCheckGuardFrag`, `outputAttributesFrag`'s Include/mapConcat broadcast) but projects the nine
  histogram columns instead of one Value, with the merge fold applied to the per-pair joined columns
  instead of per-group arrays.

Both are real cross-package `chplan`/`chsql` design work with real risk to the shared join emitter; this
part is not a small extension the way `on()`/`ignoring()` is.

### Recommendation

Split this issue: `on()`/`ignoring()` for `+`/`-`/`==`/`!=` (one-to-one only) is a well-scoped, low-risk
follow-up PR using the shape above. `group_left()`/`group_right()` should stay a separate, larger effort —
it's the part that actually needs the `chplan.VectorJoin` generalization / dedicated join node this issue
originally called out.

title: promql: and/or/unless between two exponential-histogram selectors is rejected
body:
## What's missing

Reference Prometheus's vector set operators (`and`, `or`, `unless`) match purely on labels — they never
inspect whether a matched sample is float-valued or a native histogram, so
`demo_latency_exp_hist and demo_latency_exp_hist` (and the `or` / `unless` forms) are valid upstream
regardless of `demo_latency_exp_hist` being an exponential-histogram metric.

Cerberus rejects every such query today. `internal/promql/lower.go`'s `lowerRoot` only special-cases the
value-combining shapes for two exp-histogram-valued operands — `+`/`-` (`histogram_native_binop.go`) and
`==`/`!=` (`histogram_native_binop_eq.go`) — plus the comparison operators reference itself forbids
(`*`, `/`, `^`, `%`, `atan2`, `>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=`, answered empty per #2313). `and` / `or` / `unless`
match none of those recognisers, so both operands fall through to the generic vector-selector lowering
path, which hits `expHistogramSelectorRouting`'s catch-all rejection
(`internal/promql/lower.go:expHistogramSelectorRouting`, message: `"%q is an exponential histogram
metric; only a bare %q selector, sum()/avg()/count() over one, rate()/increase()/delta()/irate()/
idelta()/sum_over_time()/avg_over_time()/resets()/changes() over one, histogram_quantile(),
histogram_count(), histogram_sum(), and the %q/%q companion selectors are supported"`).

Verified directly by lowering `demo_latency_exp_hist and demo_latency_exp_hist` against
`schema.DefaultOTelMetrics()` via `promql.LowerAtRange` — it fails with exactly that message.

## Why this is a separate issue from #2273

#2273 tracks vector-matching modifiers (`on()`/`ignoring()`/`group_left()`/`group_right()`) plus `==`/`!=`
for the two *value-combining* shapes (`+`/`-` and `==`/`!=`). Those are now precisely represented by their
own dedicated rejection sites (`histogram_native_binop.go:lowerExpHistogramHistogramBinop#f9a375de` and
`histogram_native_binop_eq.go:lowerExpHistogramHistogramCompareBinop#f3d0ee83`), both already tracking

title: promql: group_left()/group_right() still unsupported for exp-histogram binops
body:
## What's still missing after this change

The PR closing most of #2273 answers `on()`/`ignoring()` one-to-one matching for
`+`/`-` and `==`/`!=` between two exponential-histogram selectors, and the `bool`
modifier for `==`/`!=`. `group_left()`/`group_right()` (many-to-one broadcast) is
explicitly carved out and still rejected:

```
promql: group_left()/group_right() matching is not yet supported for binary
arithmetic between two exponential histogram selectors; only one-to-one matching
(default, on(), or ignoring()) is supported
```

(and the analogous message for `==`/`!=`).

## Why it's a separate lift

Reference Prometheus's `group_left(<labels>)` / `group_right(<labels>)` broadcast
the "one" side's matched histogram onto every row of the "many" side sharing the
match key, optionally copying `<labels>` from the "one" side onto the "many"
side's output (the `Include` list). The current histogram merge/compare shape
(`internal/promql/histogram_native_binop.go`'s `mergeTwoHistogramProjections`,
`internal/promql/histogram_native_binop_eq.go`'s `compareTwoHistogramProjections`)
is a `UnionAll` of the two operands feeding one `Aggregate` grouped by the match
key with a `count() = 2` Having guard standing in for a one-to-one INNER JOIN —
that shape has no way to express "N rows on one side, 1 row on the other,
broadcast the one row's histogram onto each of the N."

`internal/chsql/vector_join.go`'s `emitVectorJoin` already implements this
broadcast for plain float-valued `chplan.VectorJoin` (the `CardManyToOne` /
`CardOneToMany` branches: the "many" side keeps per-series granularity via
`argMax`, the "one" side collapses to one row per match key with the same
`throwIf(uniqExact(Attributes) > 1, ...)` guard `on()`/`ignoring()` matching now
uses for the histogram case too, via
`internal/promql/histogram_native_binop_match.go`'s
`applyVectorMatchToHistogramOperand`). Extending this to histogram-valued rows
needs either:

- generalizing `chplan.VectorJoin` to carry a histogram payload (nine columns)
  per side instead of a single `Value` float, so the existing broadcast +
  `Include`-overlay machinery in `internal/chsql/vector_join.go` can be reused
  for a histogram merge instead of a scalar op, or
- a dedicated histogram-aware join node mirroring `VectorJoin`'s per-side
  aggregation + uniqueness-guard shape, with its own emitter path.

Either is a materially larger change than the on()/ignoring() one-to-one case
(which reused the existing merge/compare Aggregate unchanged, just pre-processing
each operand independently) — it touches the join SHAPE itself, not just the
match-key computation feeding into it.

## Scope

Both `+`/`-` (`internal/promql/histogram_native_binop.go`) and `==`/`!=`
(`internal/promql/histogram_native_binop_eq.go`, including the `bool` modifier
variant) share the same gap and the same `isSupportedHistogramMatchCardinality`
gate, so one design/implementation should close all of them together.

title: Pixel MP4 capture time depends on upload client; Android timeline and asset info can disagree
body: ### Description ## What happened? The same Google Pixel MP4 is handled differently by Ente depending on **which client performs the initial upload**. I recorded a short test video on a **Google Pixel 7** at approximately **12:39 CEST (UTC+02:00)** on 16 August 2026. The MP4 contains a QuickTime creation timestamp of: ```text 2026:08:16 10:39:22 ``` This corresponds to approximately **12:39:22 CEST**. I then tested the same video through two different Ente upload paths. ## Result matrix ```text Same Pixel MP4 Actual local capture time: ~12:39 CEST QuickTime CreateDate: 10:39 UTC-style value INITIAL UPLOAD: Android ---------------------------------------------- Viewed in Android: Timeline position: ~12:39 CORRECT Asset information: ~12:39 CORRECT Viewed in Linux Desktop: Timeline position: ~12:39 CORRECT Asset information: ~12:39 CORRECT INITIAL UPLOAD: Linux Desktop ---------------------------------------------- Viewed in Linux Desktop: Timeline position: 10:39 WRONG Asset information: 10:39 WRONG Viewed in Android: Timeline position: ~12:39 CORRECT Asset information: 10:39 WRONG ``` So the exact same Pixel MP4 can become either a fully correct asset or an incorrectly timestamped asset depending on which Ente client performs the initial upload. There is also an additional inconsistency: For the copy initially uploaded by Desktop, **Android places it at the correct ~12:39 position in the timeline, while Android's own asset-information panel still reports 10:39**. This suggests that different parts of Ente are not using the same timestamp-resolution logic. ## Steps to reproduce 1. Record an MP4 video using a Google Pixel while in a timezone different from UTC. 2. In my test, the phone was in **Europe during CEST (UTC+02:00)**. 3. Upload the original video directly using Ente Photos Android. 4. View the resulting asset in: - Ente Android - Ente Desktop 5. Record the timeline position and asset-information time. 6. Upload the same MP4 using Ente Photos Desktop for Linux. 7. Again view that resulting asset in: - Ente Desktop - Ente Android 8. Compare the timeline position and asset-information time. In my reproduction: ```text Actual local capture time: ~12:39 CEST QuickTime CreateDate: 10:39 UTC-style value Android-uploaded copy: Android timeline: ~12:39 Android info: ~12:39 Desktop timeline: ~12:39 Desktop info: ~12:39 Desktop-uploaded copy: Desktop timeline: 10:39 Desktop info: 10:39 Android timeline: ~12:39 Android info: 10:39 ``` I have screenshots showing these results. ## Expected behavior The same media file should resolve to the same capture time regardless of: - which Ente client performs the initial upload - which Ente client later displays the asset - whether the time is used for timeline placement or shown in asset information For this file, the correct local capture time is approximately **12:39 CEST**, not 10:39. The Android-uploaded copy demonstrates that Ente is capable of resolving this file to the correct local capture time. The Desktop-uploaded copy demonstrates that the Desktop ingestion path resolves it differently. The fact that Android later places the Desktop-uploaded copy correctly in the timeline while still showing 10:39 in asset information suggests that Android's timeline and asset-information views may use different timestamp logic. ## Relevant metadata Relevant metadata from the untouched Pixel MP4: ```text [QuickTime] CreateDate : 2026:08:16 10:39:22 [QuickTime] ModifyDate : 2026:08:16 10:39:22 [Track1] TrackCreateDate : 2026:08:16 10:39:22 [Track1] TrackModifyDate : 2026:08:16 10:39:22 [Track1] MediaCreateDate : 2026:08:16 10:39:22 [Track1] MediaModifyDate : 2026:08:16 10:39:22 [Keys] AndroidModel : Pixel 7 [Keys] AndroidManufacturer : Google ``` The other tracks contain the same `10:39:22` creation/modification timestamp. Importantly, the Pixel MP4 has **no timezone-aware `Keys:CreationDate` field**. SHA-256 of the test video: ```text 0e981fd6e87783e484a7fad176a5cd96e664c1bec58f2a61e77806fd73d12159 ``` I have intentionally omitted GPS/location metadata and unrelated container/media information from this report. ## iPhone comparison I also compared this behavior with an iPhone video. The iPhone video contains both an ordinary QuickTime timestamp and a timezone-aware local creation timestamp, for example: ```text [QuickTime] CreateDate : 2026:04:20 08:48:08 [Keys] CreationDate : 2026:04:20 20:46:37+12:00 ``` Ente handles the iPhone video correctly. By comparison, Pixel videos contain the QuickTime UTC-style timestamps but do not appear to include `Keys:CreationDate`. ## Additional experiment / possible clue As an experiment, I made a copy of an affected Android/Pixel-style MP4 and added only a timezone-aware `Keys:CreationDate`, while preserving all existing QuickTime, track and media timestamps. For example: ```text QuickTime CreateDate : 2026:04:07 23:12:55 Keys CreationDate : 2026:04:08 11:12:55+12:00 ``` After uploading this modified copy, Ente displayed the correct local time and placed the video correctly in the timeline on both Android and Linux Desktop. This may be a useful clue for debugging fallback behavior when `Keys:CreationDate` is absent. However, the main reproducible bug is that the **same unmodified Pixel MP4 receives different capture-time treatment depending on whether Android or Desktop performs the initial upload**. ## Environment ```text Ente Photos Android: 1.3.61 Android device: Google Pixel 7 Ente Photos Desktop: 1.7.27 Desktop platform: Linux Timezone during test: Europe Local timezone: CEST / UTC+02:00 Test date: 2026-08-16 ``` ## Why this matters This affects automatic backup of videos from Google Pixel phones. The same Pixel MP4 can end up with different capture-time behavior depending on the upload path: - direct Android upload produces a correct asset - Desktop upload produces a wrong capture time - Android can later place that Desktop-uploaded asset correctly in the timeline while still displaying the wrong time in asset information This is particularly problematic for Desktop watch-folder workflows, because Pixel videos uploaded by Desktop may be placed at the wrong chronological position even though Ente Android can correctly interpret the same file. ## Attachments - screenshot of timeline on android showing both videos placed correctly (despite one having the wrong time) - screenshot of timeline on linux desktop showing incorrect placement ### Version v1.3.61 and v.1.7.27 ### What product are you using? Ente Photos ### What platform are you using? Mobile - Android, Desktop - Linux

title: opa-utils ScoreUtil is a process-wide singleton — stale resource data corrupts risk scores after the first scan in a long-lived process
body:
## Summary

`score.NewScore()` in the vendored `github.com/kubescape/opa-utils` package (pinned in `go.mod`) uses `sync.Once` to build a package-level singleton. The first call in a process sets its internal `resources` map from that call's argument; every subsequent call in the same process — regardless of what's passed in — returns the *same* object, still holding the first call's data.


## Where kubescape hits this

`core/pkg/score/score.go`'s `NewScoreWrapper` calls `score.NewScore(opaSessionObj.AllResources)` directly. Its `Calculate(EPostureReportV2)` — the path every scan uses — calls `CalculatePostureReportV2`, which consults the (possibly stale) `resources` map to compute `report.SummaryDetails.Score` and `Frameworks[i].Score` (the legacy risk score, exposed via the JSON printer's top-level `score` field and `ResultsHandler.GetRiskScore()`).

Any process that scans more than once hits this — most concretely `httphandler`, a persistent server that handles repeated `/v1/scan` requests without restarting.

## How this was tested

Wrote a standalone reproduction importing the real vendored `opa-utils/score` package at the exact version kubescape pins (v0.0.307), calling `NewScore()` twice with two different resource maps (simulating two separate scans in one process) and comparing the returned pointers. Ran it for real against the actual dependency, not a mock.

```go
resourcesA := map[string]workloadinterface.IMetadata{"scan-A-resource": nil}
resourcesB := map[string]workloadinterface.IMetadata{"scan-B-resource": nil}

su1 := score.NewScore(resourcesA)
su2 := score.NewScore(resourcesB)
// su1 == su2
```

## Real output

```
First scan:  NewScore(resourcesA) -> 0x63d0c7132150
Second scan: NewScore(resourcesB) -> 0x63d0c7132150

BUG CONFIRMED: su1 == su2 (same pointer).
The second scan's resource map (resourcesB) was silently discarded;
NewScore() returned the FIRST scan's ScoreUtil instance instead.
```

## Impact

`ComplianceScore` (used for `--compliance-threshold` CI gating) is unaffected — it's computed independently from pass/fail counts, not from `resources`. But the legacy risk `Score` field, shown in output and used by any consumer of `GetRiskScore()`, silently reflects a *different, earlier* scan's resource weights (replica counts, DaemonSet node counts, etc.) for every scan after the first in a long-lived process — with no error, since resource-ID lookups against the wrong map just miss silently rather than crash.

## Suggested fix

The root cause lives in `kubescape/opa-utils`, not this repo — the real fix is removing the `sync.Once`/package-global pattern there so each `ScoreUtil` instance owns its own `resources`, matching what the vendor code's own comment already says should happen. `core/pkg/score/score.go` could carry a narrower workaround in the meantime (e.g. not relying on the shared instance across sessions), but filing here first since this is where the impact was found and reproduced.

title: Scanned resource names passed as a Printf format string corrupt terminal report output
body:
## Summary

`cautils.SimpleDisplay`/`StarDisplay` (`core/cautils/display.go`) both do `fmt.Fprintf(w, format, a...)`, treating their second argument as the format string. Several call sites in the pretty-printer pass already-built, resource-derived text (embedding `resource.GetKind()`/`GetName()` straight from a scanned manifest) as that argument, with zero variadic args:

```go
// core/pkg/resultshandling/printer/v2/prettyprinter.go:293
cautils.SimpleDisplay(pp.writer, resources[i]+"\n")
```

File and repo scans parse YAML directly with no Kubernetes admission validation, so a crafted manifest can set `metadata.name` (or any field that ends up in that string) to contain `%s`, `%d`, etc.

## How this was tested

Wrote a standalone reproduction calling the real `cautils.SimpleDisplay` function directly (not a mock), passing a resource name shaped exactly like the real call site does, then compared the actual output against the real name. Ran it for real against the current code.

## output

```
Resource name in manifest: "my-deployment-%s-%d-leaked"
Actual report output:      "my-deployment-%!s(MISSING)-%!d(MISSING)-leaked\n"
```

## Impact

A resource name containing `%`-verbs renders corrupted in the terminal report instead of the actual name — a report-integrity bug, not memory-unsafe, but concretely triggerable from untrusted scan input (a malicious repo scanned via CI/PR automation, a common kubescape workflow). This makes it harder to tell which resource a failed control is actually attributed to.

Affected call sites (same pattern, all pass pre-built resource-derived strings as the format argument):
- `core/pkg/resultshandling/printer/v2/prettyprinter.go:293`
- `core/pkg/resultshandling/printer/v2/prettyprinter/utils.go:202`
- `core/pkg/resultshandling/printer/v2/prettyprinter/reposcan.go:77-78`
- `core/pkg/resultshandling/printer/v2/prettyprinter/clusterscan.go:76-77`

## Suggested fix

Always pass user-derived text as a variadic argument with a literal `"%s"` format string, e.g. `cautils.SimpleDisplay(pp.writer, "%s\n", resources[i])`, never as the format parameter itself.

title: Case-sensitive output-extension check duplicated across every v2 printer doubles the extension (Report.JSON -> Report.JSON.json)
body:
## Summary

Every printer in `core/pkg/resultshandling/printer/v2/` reimplements the same output-extension check, case-sensitive against a lowercase constant, with no shared helper:

```go
// jsonprinter.go:43-45 (same pattern in yamlprinter.go, sarifprinter.go,
// gitlabsastprinter.go, junit.go, htmlprinter.go, pdf.go, markdownprinter.go,
// csvprinter.go, prettyprinter.go)
if filepath.Ext(strings.TrimSpace(outputFile)) != printer.JsonOutputExt {
    outputFile = outputFile + printer.JsonOutputExt
}
```

`--output Report.JSON` (or `.SARIF`, `.HTML`, `.PDF`, `.XML`, differently-cased for any format) fails this equality check and gets a second, redundant lowercase extension appended.

Related prior art: #2292 fixed the identical class of bug on the *input* side (case-sensitive detection of `.YAML`/`.Json` manifest files being scanned). This report is about the *output* side (`--output`/`SetWriter`), which was never addressed by that fix and lives in entirely separate code.

## How this was tested

Wrote a standalone reproduction calling the real `JsonPrinter.SetWriter` directly against a temp directory with `--output Report.JSON`, then inspected what file actually landed on disk. Ran it for real against the current code, not a mock.

##  output

Actual file(s) created on disk:

title: HTML report always fetches its logo from a live, unpinned GitHub URL instead of embedding it
body: ## Summary Unlike the PDF printer, which embeds its logo at build time via `//go:embed logo.png`, the HTML report template references a live, branch-tracking GitHub URL: ```html ``` Every time a generated HTML report is opened in a browser — including from a CI artifact days or months later, or in an air-gapped/offline compliance environment — it makes an outbound request to GitHub. ## How this was tested - Confirmed the URL is genuinely live: `curl -sI` returns `HTTP/2 200`. - Confirmed `master` is a moving branch reference, not a pinned commit or tag: `git ls-remote https://github.com/kubescape/kubescape.git master` currently resolves to a specific, different-every-time commit SHA, so the asset behind this URL is not fixed to what existed when any given report was generated. - Confirmed the contrast with the PDF printer, which embeds the identical logo via `//go:embed logo.png` rather than fetching it. ## output ``` $ curl -sI https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubescape/kubescape/master/core/pkg/resultshandling/printer/v2/pdf/logo.png HTTP/2 200 content-type: image/png ... $ git ls-remote https://github.com/kubescape/kubescape.git master 3c7fd6af1379e39413c6910163f13ffe0c1e96ef refs/heads/master ``` ## Impact - Leaks the fact/time/IP that a potentially sensitive security report was viewed, to GitHub, every time it's opened. - Breaks (shows a broken image) when viewed offline or in an air-gapped environment — a real scenario for compliance report review. - Not version-pinned: the asset behind `master` can change or the file can be moved/renamed, silently altering or 404ing old reports with no way to know in advance. ## Suggested fix Embed the logo the same way `pdf/report_template.go` already does — `//go:embed` plus a `data:` URI in the HTML template — removing the external dependency entirely.

title: Add rule: detect subjects that can modify nodes/status
body:
# Description
Kubescape currently has no rule detecting subjects with permissions to modify `nodes/status` subresources.

A subject with `update` or `patch` permissions on `nodes/status` can alter node labels and conditions, allowing them to bypass workload scheduling constraints (`nodeSelector`, `nodeAffinity`) designed to keep sensitive pods isolated from untrusted nodes.

# Environment
OS: `N/A`
Version: `main`

# Steps To Reproduce
1. Create a `Role` or `ClusterRole` granting `update` or `patch` permissions on `nodes/status` (or wildcard forms `*/status`, `*`) in the core API group.
2. Bind the role to a subject via a `ClusterRoleBinding` (or `RoleBinding`).
3. Run a Kubescape RBAC scan.
4. Observe that no rule/control fails.

# Expected behavior
Kubescape should flag subjects with permissions to update or patch `nodes/status` subresources.

# Actual Behavior
Permissions modifying `nodes/status` are ignored, allowing scheduling constraint bypass vectors to go undetected.

# Additional context
* **Proposed Rule:** Add `modify-node-status-v1` (ported from rbac-police's `modify_node_status` policy).
* **Aggregator:** Uses `subject-role-rolebinding` to flag `update`/`patch`/`*` on `nodes/status` (including `*/status` and `*` wildcards) in the core API group.
* **Separation of Concerns:** Kept separate from `pods/status` and `services/status` due to differing exploit scopes and severity levels (Low).
* Follow-up to #3097.

title: circleci config process should print jobs available and their parameters
body:
## What problem does this feature solve?:
<!---
  Describe the use-case in which this feature would be used or required.
-->

I want to test parameterized jobs from the circleci CLI without having to figure out which auto-generated job name to use. 

Why is this a cumbersome limitation: 

`circleci config process` generates one job in the output for each parametrized job that appears in the workflow. 

Eg if job A accepts parameter B, and workflow specifies two jobs that use A, with B values "abc" and "def", then the output will have a job named `A-1` which is job A with B=abc, and another job named `A-2` which is job A with B=def. 

Unfortunately, which auto-generated job corresponds to the desired combination of values of job parameters that I want to test can only be inferred by finding which generated job code has the values I want, rather error-prone. 

Only once I know the generated job naem will I be able to run eg `circleci local execute A-1`. 

Solution: 

`circleci config process` should output which job names were generated, and what were the job parameters used for each one
it should therefore not output to stdout, instead it should require a file name.

## Provide an example:
<!---
  Show an example how how this command may be used, and what output you expect to receive.
-->

In `config.yml`, say I have this: 
```
jobs:
  deploy:
    parameters:
      env_name:
        type: string
        default: devops1
    docker:
      - image: cimg/base:2021.07
        user: root
    steps:
      - checkout
      - run:
          name: Deploy to << parameters.env_name >>
          command: ls 

workflows:
  version: 2.1

  auto-deployments:
    jobs:
      - deploy:
          env_name: dev
      - deploy:
          env_name: dev2
```

then `circleci config process INFILE --out OUTFILE` would create OUTFILE instead of outputting it to stdout, AND stdout would show something like this instead: 
```
$ circleci config process .circleci/config.yml --out /tmp/cci-config-processed.yml
auto-generated jobs:
  deploy-1:
    env_name: dev
  deploy-2:
    env_name: dev2
```
Then I would automatically know that `circleci local execute --job deploy-1` will test `deploy` with parameter `env_name` = `dev`
comments:
So I found out in section https://circleci.com/docs/2.0/reusing-config/#authoring-parameterized-jobs of docs that the job name can be overridden in the workflow in the config file, in which case the job names do not need to be output. 

However I must say that it is rather counter-intuitive that job names get determined by workflows, since the CLI docs are clear that workflows are not supported in CLI. 

So I think this should be converted to a bug report: 

- the note on that [page](https://circleci.com/docs/2.0/reusing-config/#authoring-parameterized-jobs) is really easy to miss, it should be made more obvious (perhaps closer to the beginning of that page), and in fact it should be recommended to override the name... seriously seeing a job named deploy-1 and deploy-2 in circleci window should be avoided
- actually parametrized jobs should probably *require* that the name be overridden. 
- the docs for circleci *CLI* should have a short paragraph about job names of parametrized jobs, and how their names are generated from workflows, it should link to the above section, and should explain how the overridden name is what must be used

It seems like you're mistakenly trying to correlate job names as being some kind of job instance hash.

I'd imagine this isn't going to be as helpful as you think it will and that functionality should exist in some other property.

body:
## Meta:

**CircleCI CLI Version:**

`0.1.23391+5cbf90e (homebrew)` (Mac) and `0.1.23241` (Linux)

**Operating System:**

MacOS and Linux

---

## Current behavior:

If you have config like this:
```yaml
version: 2.1

jobs:
  job1:
    docker:
      - image: cimg/base
    steps:
      - run: echo hello
  job2:
    docker:
      - image: cimg/base
    steps:
      - run: echo world
 
parameters:
  run_invalid:
    type: boolean
    default: false

workflows:
  invalid:
    when: << pipeline.parameters.run_invalid >>
    jobs:
      - job1:
          name: job_renamed
      - job2:
          requires:
            - job1 # Error is here, should be `job_renamed`
```

`circleci config validate` says the config is valid, even though it's not.

A real-world failure: https://app.circleci.com/pipelines/github/color/color/275733

## Expected behavior:

`circleci config validate` should flag the invalid job name in the `requires`.

## When did this begin / Was this previously working?:

Unsure

## Additional Information:

The config is properly flagged as invalid if I flip the default value of `run_invalid` from `false` to `true`
comments:
## Triage: still reproduces on the v1 CLI, and this is now the canonical issue

Re-ran your exact config against the rewritten v1 CLI:

```console
$ circleci config validate -c config.yml
Config file at "config.yml" is valid.
```

Still valid, still wrong — `job2` requires `job1`, which was renamed to `job_renamed`.

**Consolidating #1077 into this one.** It reports the same mechanism with a different
`when` form (`equal: [test2, << pipeline.parameters.run-job >>]` where `run-job` defaults
to `test`), and makes the impact point well:

> If one has many "non default" workflow parameters defined, they break with such missing
> dependencies and the periodically scheduled triggers fail.

That is the real cost — the breakage lands on a scheduled trigger days later, not on the
push that introduced it.

#577 was the adjacent symptom (validation *erroring* with "All Workflows have been
filtered from this Pipeline" when every workflow was gated) and is fixed in v1: the CLI
now supplies a full set of local pipeline values, so such configs validate. But
supplying values means the gated workflow evaluates to "skipped", and a skipped workflow's
job graph is never checked. Hence this bug survives.

**Where the fix has to happen:** the CLI sends the config to the compile endpoint and
reports the verdict; it does not implement the check. So this needs the config-compilation
service to validate the job graph of every declared workflow regardless of whether its
`when` evaluates true for the supplied values. Routing it that way internally.

**Workaround in the meantime**, since scheduled triggers are where this bites: validate
once per parameter combination that a trigger can produce. v1 lets you set the values
without editing the config —

```sh
circleci config process .circleci/config.yml --pipeline-parameters 'run-job: test2'
```

— so a CI step that loops over the enum values will catch a bad `requires` before the
schedule does.

comments:
## Triage: confirming where this needs to be fixed

You are right that the Dockerfiles are the problem, and worth being explicit that they are
on the **`v0` branch** — `Dockerfile` and `Dockerfile.alpine`, which build the published
`circleci/circleci-cli` images that `orb-tools@12` jobs run in. The git in those base
images predates blobless-clone support (`--filter=blob:none`, git 2.19+), which is what
CircleCI's checkout step now uses.

The v1 CLI (`main`) does not publish a Docker image at all — it ships as native packages
(Homebrew, Chocolatey, winget, Snap, deb) and archives. So this is not a v1 bug, and it is
not something the rewrite fixes for you.

Keeping this open as a `v0` packaging fix, which qualifies as the kind of critical fix that
branch still takes: rebase both Dockerfiles onto a base image with a current git. That
unblocks `orb-tools/lint`, `pack`, `review` and `continue` for everyone on orb-tools@12,
not just this report.

Unrelated aside, since your config shows `exclude: RC006  # GitHub repository is private` —
making RC006/RC007 work for private repos is #816, which lives in
[orb-tools-orb](https://github.com/CircleCI-Public/orb-tools-orb) rather than here.
