title: orb validate rejects parameter expressions in fields with regex value-pattern validation
body:
## Summary

`circleci orb validate` (CLI 0.1.34950) rejects valid orb authoring patterns that put a `<< parameters.X >>` placeholder into a string field whose schema has a `pattern:` (regex) value check. The validator runs the regex against the literal placeholder string instead of deferring it until after parameter substitution. Integer parameters work fine because their schema skips the pattern step.

## Reproducer

[orb-tools/pack failure on cypress-io/circleci-orb#577](https://app.circleci.com/pipelines/gh/cypress-io/circleci-orb/2179/workflows/ba990d9c-bf5e-4b70-a3bd-0bc5e355881d) — minimal repro is a `run` step with both keys threaded from parameters:

```yaml
parameters:
  max-auto-reruns:
    type: integer
    default: 0
  auto-rerun-delay:
    type: string
    default: "0s"
steps:
  - run:
      command: << parameters.cypress-command >>
      max_auto_reruns: << parameters.max-auto-reruns >>     # passes
      auto_rerun_delay: << parameters.auto-rerun-delay >>   # FAILS
```

## Failure

```
[#/commands/run-tests/steps/1/run/auto_rerun_delay]
  string [<< parameters.auto-rerun-delay >>]
  does not match pattern ^((10|[1-9])m|([1-9][0-9]*)s)$
```

The cascading errors above this line ("extraneous key [run] is not permitted", "expected type: String, found: Mapping") are the validator's confused fallback after the run-step subschema fails to match — the root cause is the single `auto_rerun_delay` regex check.

## Expected behavior

Either:
- Defer regex/pattern checks until after parameter substitution, OR
- Recognize `<< parameters.X >>` (and other [parameter expression syntax](https://circleci.com/docs/reusing-config/#using-the-parameters-declaration)) as a valid placeholder for any string field with a `pattern:` constraint.

The existing integer handling (passes `<< parameters.max-auto-reruns >>` cleanly when the field is typed `integer`) is the right precedent.

## Workaround

Drop the parameter and hardcode the value in the orb, or omit it and rely on the runtime default. This is what cypress-io/circleci-orb#577 ended up doing.

## Affects

- CircleCI CLI 0.1.34950 (latest at filing)
- Any orb author who wants to expose a parameter for a string field that has `pattern:` validation in the orb schema (`auto_rerun_delay`, possibly other recently-added timing/duration fields).

## Environment

- macOS 15.4 (Darwin 25.4.0)
- `circleci version` → `0.1.34950+8ff907b (homebrew)`
comments:
Found a second, related manifestation of the same root cause while working around the original report.

## Reproducer 2

Using the integer-typed `max_auto_reruns` field — which I called out in the original report as "works fine" — actually has the same problem when the parameter defaults to `0`:

```yaml
# In an orb command:
parameters:
  max-auto-reruns:
    type: integer
    default: 0
steps:
  - run:
      command: << parameters.cypress-command >>
      max_auto_reruns: << parameters.max-auto-reruns >>
```

When this orb is consumed in a config that doesn't override the parameter, validation fails with:

```
[#/jobs/<JobName>/steps/N/run/max_auto_reruns] 0 is not greater or equal to 1
```

The validator substitutes the parameter's default value (`0`), then runs the field's value-schema check (`minimum: 1`) on the substituted result. The schema constraint is correct per [the docs](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/orchestrate/automatic-reruns/) ("a value between 1 and 5") — the issue is that an orb author has no way to expose the field as an *opt-in* parameter, because the natural "off" sentinel (`0`, or any value outside `[1, 5]`) fails validation even when the consumer never intends the parameter to be active.

## Reproducer

[orb-tools/continue failure on cypress-io/circleci-orb#577 (pipeline 2180)](https://app.circleci.com/pipelines/gh/cypress-io/circleci-orb/2180) — 56 schema violations, all the same root cause across every `cypress/run` instantiation in `test-deploy.yml`.

## Workaround

Fork the step into `when:` / `unless:` variants:

```yaml
- unless:
    condition: << parameters.max-auto-reruns >>
    steps:
      - run:
          command: << parameters.cypress-command >>
- when:
    condition: << parameters.max-auto-reruns >>
    steps:
      - run:
          command: << parameters.cypress-command >>
          max_auto_reruns: << parameters.max-auto-reruns >>
```

The `unless` branch (taken at validation time when the default is `0`) never includes the field, so the value-schema check never runs against `0`. Ugly but works. Applied in cypress-io/circleci-orb#577.

## Suggested fix

Same as the original ask — defer value-schema checks (both `pattern:` for strings and `minimum:`/`maximum:` for integers) until after parameter substitution. That would let orb authors expose any field as a parameter without having to fork the step structure to handle the "field absent" case.

title: Expose the UI's "Rerun failed tests" action from the CLI
body:
The job page in the web UI offers four rerun actions. Only two of them have a CLI equivalent:

| Web UI action | CLI equivalent |
| --- | --- |
| Rerun workflow from start | `circleci workflow rerun <workflow-id>` |
| Rerun workflow from failed | `circleci workflow rerun <workflow-id> --from-failed` |
| **Rerun failed tests** | **none** |
| Rerun job with SSH | none |

This request is about the third one.

## Why it matters

Today we do this in the web UI. What we'd like is for the whole triage loop to run through the MCP server that wraps this CLI: an agent can already read the failures (`circleci testresult list <job-id>` defaults to failures only) and can rerun jobs, but it has no way to act on that read with the narrowest rerun available. The natural next step after "one test failed, here's the error" is "rerun just that test", and it's the one step in the loop that has to happen by hand in a browser.

The nearest CLI option, `--from-failed`, is job-granular: it re-dispatches each failed job in full. On a suite where one test fails out of 12,546, that means re-running all 12,546 tests — around nine minutes of compute — to re-check a single failure.

## Proposed shape

Either a flag on the existing command:

```
circleci workflow rerun <workflow-id> --failed-tests
```

or a job-scoped subcommand, which sits closer to where the action lives in the UI:

```
circleci job rerun <job-id> --failed-tests
```

Either works for us. The job-scoped form composes more naturally with `circleci testresult list <job-id>`, which is already addressed by job ID.

## Notes

- Version: `1.0.45973-pre`.
- I appreciate this isn't a pure control-plane operation the way `--from-failed` is — it presumably requires the job to have run its tests through CircleCI's test orchestration. title: No global machine-readable output flag
body:
## The issue

Right now the CLI only prints human-friendly text. That's great when you're
reading it in a terminal, but painful the moment you try to automate anything.

If I want a pipeline to fail on a bad config, I run `circleci config validate`
and get a paragraph of text back. To act on it in a script, I have to grep the
output and hope the wording never changes. It does change, and then my
automation quietly breaks. The exit code tells me pass or fail, but not *what*
went wrong in a way a machine can read.

## What I'd like

A single global flag: `-o, --output json` (default stays `text`, so nothing
breaks). In JSON mode, commands return a predictable shape like:

```json
{
  "status": "error",
  "errors": [
    { "code": "invalid_key", "message": "unexpected key 'jobz'", "path": ".jobz", "line": 4 }
  ],
  "warnings": []
}
```

Nice-to-have: honor a `CIRCLECI_CLI_OUTPUT=json` env var so CI can default to it
without adding the flag everywhere.

## Commands it should cover

`config validate`, `config pack`, `orb validate`, `orb list`, `context list`,
and the `runner` commands.

## Why it matters

It turns `config validate` into a reliable CI gate and lets dashboards or
ChatOps surface line-level errors without brittle text parsing. Small change,
big quality-of-life win for anyone running the CLI in automation.

BR,
Arman.
comments:
## Triage: partly shipped in the v1 CLI — narrowing this to what is left

Thanks Arman, this was one of the founding requirements of the v1 rewrite (`main`; `v0` is
the legacy CLI that ships today), and most of it is in.

**Done.** Every data-returning command takes `--json`, with its fields enumerated in
`--help` so you can see the shape without running it. That is a hard rule for the v1
codebase, not a per-command decision, so the coverage list in your report —
`config validate`, `config pack`, `orb validate`, `orb list`, `context list`, the `runner`
commands — is covered, along with everything else. Streams are separated properly too:
data on stdout, progress and diagnostics on stderr, so `circleci ... --json | jq` is safe.

Errors already carry structure internally — every one has a code, title, message,
suggestions and a docs reference, and exits with a meaningful code (2 bad arguments,
3 auth, 4 API, 5 not found, 7 validation failure, 8 timeout). So `config validate` as a CI
gate works on the exit code today without grepping prose.

**Still open, and what I am keeping this issue for:**

1. **Structured errors in JSON mode.** The error type has the fields; `--json` does not yet
   render them. Your example shape is close to what we would emit — `status`, `errors[]`
   with `code`/`message`, `warnings[]` — with the caveat that per-error `path` and `line`
   come from the config-compilation service, so line-level detail depends on what it
   returns rather than on the CLI alone.
2. **`-o, --output json` as a global alias for `--json`.** Worth doing for the reason you
   give: one flag you can pass to anything, rather than remembering which commands have it.
3. **An environment variable.** `CIRCLECI_CLI_OUTPUT` in your report — v1 uses the
   `CIRCLE_` prefix (`CIRCLE_TOKEN`, `CIRCLE_HOST`, `CIRCLE_NO_COLOR`), so this would be
   `CIRCLE_OUTPUT=json`, documented in `circleci help environment`.

Of those, (1) is the one that unblocks the dashboards-and-ChatOps case you describe; (2)
and (3) are ergonomics.

Thanks @pete-woods 
I’m excited to see an amazing version ahead!
BR

title: circleci local execute will not be reimplemented in the v1 CLI
body:
## Summary

`circleci local execute` will not be reimplemented in the v1 CLI. This issue explains
why, and records what we suggest instead. Every open `local execute` issue is being
closed as *not planned* and linked here.

## Why it is going away

`local execute` was never a self-contained feature of this CLI. The CLI was a thin
launcher: it pulled the `circleci/picard` image and handed your config to a copy of
our internal **build-agent** running inside it. Almost everything people report against
`local execute` — checkout, caching, workspaces, SSH keys, `store_test_results`,
networking, cgroups — is build-agent behaviour, not CLI behaviour.

That arrangement stopped working properly some time ago:

- **The build-agent it launches is pinned to a very old version.** The image digest is
  hardcoded (see [`local/local.go`](https://github.com/CircleCI-Public/circleci-cli/blob/v0/local/local.go)),
  so `Fetching latest build environment...` fetches an artifact that is years old and
  no longer matches how jobs actually run on CircleCI. Newer build-agent images no
  longer ship the subcommand the CLI invokes, so `--build-agent-version` does not
  rescue it either (see #1130).
- **The environment it emulates has diverged from the real one.** Docker moved to
  cgroup v2, containerd image storage, rootless daemons and Apple Silicon; Podman and
  Colima became common. Each of those is a separate open issue against a component we
  no longer build (#676, #811, #588, #1079, #464, #774).
- **The feature set was always a subset.** No `machine` executors, no workspaces, no
  caching, no contexts, no parallelism, no test-result upload. Those are the parts of
  a job most worth reproducing, and the ones a local Docker container cannot honestly
  reproduce.

Reviving it would mean taking ownership of, versioning, and shipping a public
build-agent — a much larger commitment than a CLI subcommand, and one that would still
give an approximation of the real execution environment rather than the real thing.

## What we suggest instead

**[Chunk sidecars](https://circleci.com/chunk-sidecars/)** address the same need —
validate a change before pushing — but by running it in a real CircleCI cloud
environment rather than emulating one locally. The `chunk` CLI detects your stack,
generates a Dockerfile, provisions the sidecar, and runs your configured validation
commands remotely, streaming results back.

- Docs: <https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/how-to-use-chunk-cli/>
- CLI: <https://github.com/CircleCI-Public/chunk-cli>
- Background: <https://circleci.com/blog/chunk-sidecars/>

Chunk sidecars are in Preview for Performance and Scale plans.

Two things the v1 CLI does cover that people often reached for `local execute` to get:

- **`circleci config validate` / `circleci config process`** — catch config errors,
  expand orbs and resolve parameters without running anything.
- **`circleci run watch` / `circleci job output` / `circleci testresult list`** — get
  the failure back in the terminal after a push, instead of clicking through the UI.

## Scope of this decision

- The `local` command group does not exist in the v1 CLI (`main`) and will not be added.
- The v0 implementation stays on the `v0` branch as-is; it receives critical fixes only.
- Comment here if Chunk sidecars do not cover your use case — that feedback is what
  would justify revisiting this.

title: FGA Step 5 (Intent): NanoMind classification is not reliable enough to surface on stage today
body:
## Context

The 5-step FGA model lists Step 5 as the NanoMind intent classifier — fires synchronously for HIGH-risk capabilities (up to ~800ms), asynchronously for MEDIUM, skipped for LOW. The classifier is supposed to catch the request shape that capability-only filtering misses: a syntactically-allowed action whose intent is malicious (the EchoLeak / CVE-2025-32711 pattern).

The current daemon does not reliably return the expected `attackClass` and `confidence` fields under the FGA prompt format, because:

1. The dev `nanomind-daemon` does not emit the `attackClass` field that FGA Step 5 reads (see `apps/backend/internal/application/fga_engine.go:395-404`).
2. The base SmolLM2-135M model is not fine-tuned for the daemon's prompt template; it returns repeating template tokens rather than classifications.

The result: Step 5 fails open silently in current builds. The capability-check fail-fast at Step 1 is what carries the demo today, and the talk's Beat 5 narration was explicitly amended to drop the live NanoMind classification line.

## Proposed fix (multi-stage)

1. Fix the daemon contract so it returns `attackClass` consistently, with a fallback when the model can't classify.
2. Fine-tune NanoMind on the FGA prompt format. Target an F1 above 0.85 on the OASB 4,245-sample benchmark before re-enabling the live classification line.
3. Add a Prometheus / OTel metric so operators can see Step 5's classification rate, agreement rate, and skip rate per agent.

## Related

- Demo deck (Part 3 — "Agent Runtime Conduct: 5-step FGA") lists Step 5 with the implication that it fires reliably on HIGH risk. Today it does not. This issue closes the gap between the architectural model and the running daemon.
comments: Stage 3 (Step 5 observability, AIM-side) is in PR #322. Adds `fga.intent_checks` (risk_tier / intent_mode / intent_status ∈ classified|abstain|fail_open / intent_blocked) and `fga.intent_skipped` (risk_tier) on the `aim/fga` meter, plus PromQL in OBSERVABILITY.md for classification / fail-open / skip / async-agreement rates. These quantify the silent fail-open this issue is about — they will read near-100% abstain/fail-open until Stages 1–2 land. No behavior change: the live classification/blocking line is not re-enabled. Stage 1 (daemon contract + deterministic fallback) and Stage 2 (fine-tune NanoMind to F1 > 0.85 on the OASB 4,245-sample benchmark) remain open as separate model-training work; this issue stays open until they land.

title: Verification scalability: implement local cache / batching / sidecar (v1.1 follow-up to #157)
body:
**Tracking issue for v1.1.** Carries forward the architectural work deferred from #157 (audit #39) at v1.0 cut.

## Why this was deferred from v1.0

[CHIEF-CA] DEFERRED v1.0 — see #157 close comment for the full decision block.

Short form: v1.0 launch surface is <100 agents (comfortable on the existing per-action synchronous architecture). The 5 fix options below all require 3 days to multi-week and add release risk for no day-one customer benefit.

## Capacity matrix (from #157)

| Surface | Status today |
|---------|--------------|
| 10 agents × 1 action/sec | Comfortable (demo/eval/pilot) |
| 100 agents × 5 actions/sec | Workable (small customer) |
| 1,000 agents × 10 actions/sec | Struggling (Postgres at limit) |
| 10,000 agents | Cannot serve |
| Sub-200ms p99 across regions | Cannot meet SLA |

## Re-evaluation trigger

Re-open / promote when ANY of:
- First customer registers >100 agents
- Any deployment crosses 5 actions/sec sustained
- Cross-region SLA conversation begins
- Postgres CPU on verify path crosses 50 percent sustained

## Fix options (from #157)

1. **Sidecar enforcer (OPA/SPIFFE-style, push-based revocation)** — multi-week. Highest ceiling, biggest implementation surface.
2. **Batched verification endpoint** — ~1 week. SDK contract change; needs co-release.
3. **Trust-tiered local cache with signed allow tokens** — ~2 weeks. Preserves instant-revocation semantics via short token TTL + push invalidation.
4. **Async audit pipeline (queue + batch flush)** — ~1 week. Decouples audit write from hot path; doesn't help allow/deny latency.
5. **Backend read replicas** — ~3 days. Smallest lift, doesn't fix per-action DB roundtrip, but buys headroom.

## Constraints to preserve

- Revocations propagate instantly (current invariant; #157 calls this out as "by design").
- No SDK strict-mode bypass (see audit-baseline #153 for the related strict-mode gate).
- All verification decisions remain audited.

## Related

- Original architectural defect: #157 (audit #39)

**From the release-test P2/P3 list:**

1. **Per-entry-point error-class identity.** Each entry point (`.`, `/arp`, `/express`, `/fastify`) bundles its own copy of `AIMClient` and the error classes, so `instanceof` does not match across entry points (nor across the ESM/CJS boundary). 2. **ARP disclosure text cites the `arp` CLI** (`arp telemetry log|status|opt-out`) which SDK-only consumers do not have. Now that the shim has landed and the SDK copy is canonical, reword to lead with the env-var/config opt-outs and mention the CLI as the hackmyagent-installed path.

4. **`loadCredentialsFromFile()` on a missing file throws raw `ENOENT`** instead of a typed SDK error.

title: MCP security policies are stored and editable but never evaluated
body:
## Summary

None of the four `mcp_*` security policy types are evaluated by any running code path.

`SecurityPolicyService` — the service constructed in `cmd/server/main.go` — only ever requests the
six non-MCP policy types through `policyRepo.GetByType`. `MCPPolicyEvaluator` is the sole
implementation of `mcp_allowlist`, `mcp_blocklist`, `mcp_capabilities` and `mcp_unverified`, and
nothing outside `_test.go` constructs it.

The rest of the feature did ship: the admin security-policy routes are mounted, the admin page
creates, edits and toggles all four types, and migration 052 seeded six MCP policies **enabled**,
two of them `block_and_alert` at `critical` severity. An administrator could therefore read an
enabled blocking policy and reasonably conclude connections were being blocked.

## Current state

Migration 105 disables the six seeded policies and the admin page now states plainly that MCP
policies are not enforced, so the surface no longer claims an effect that does not occur. The
evaluator is deliberately kept rather than deleted: deleting it would remove the only
implementation while leaving the UI, the CRUD API and the stored policies in place.

`TestSeededMCPPoliciesAreNotEnabled` guards against a future migration re-enabling the rows.

## Prerequisites before the evaluator can be wired

Wiring it as it stands would reject every MCP server. Any one of these is sufficient to cause
that on its own:

1. **`rules.minTrustScore` is on a 0-100 scale.** Migration 052 seeds 50 and 30 and the admin UI
   stores a percentage, but `evaluateAllowlist` compares the value against `MCPServer.TrustScore`,
   which migration 104 made canonical `[0,1]`. Every server would fall below every threshold.
2. **A bare `*` in `allowedDomains` matches no host.** `matchDomainPattern` special-cases only the
   `*.` prefix and otherwise falls through to an equality test. Seeded policies 5 and 6 use `["*"]`
   intending "allow all"; it means "allow nothing", and policy 6 is `block_and_alert`.
3. **`MCPAllowlistRules.AllowedCapabilities` is read by nothing.** An organization that configures
   it gets silent non-enforcement.

## Open design decisions

- Where the gate runs: MCP server registration, agent-to-MCP connection, a background sweep, or
  some combination. The existence of `EvaluateAllMCPServers` suggests a sweep was intended.
- Fail-open or fail-closed when evaluation itself errors. `evaluatePolicy` currently swallows
  per-policy errors and continues, which is fail-open by accident rather than by decision.
- Whether `block_and_alert` may actually block on a path that has no established block mechanism
  for MCP, or whether the first wired version is alert-only.
- Whether the six seeded defaults are re-enabled with corrected rules or left off as examples.
  Re-enabling them unchanged is wrong for reasons 1 and 2.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `rules.minTrustScore` migrated to `[0,1]` for existing rows, and the admin UI stores and
      displays it on the canonical scale.
- [ ] `matchDomainPattern` handles a bare `*`, with tests covering `*`, `*.example.com`, an exact
      host, and a non-match.
- [ ] `AllowedCapabilities` is either enforced with tests or removed from the rules type.
- [ ] The evaluator is constructed and called from a documented enforcement point.
- [ ] Fail-open versus fail-closed on evaluation error is decided explicitly and tested.
- [ ] Negative tests: a server that violates each rule type is rejected, proven to fail against
      the unwired code.
- [ ] `TestSeededMCPPoliciesAreNotEnabled` is updated or replaced, since re-enabling the seeded
      policies is expected to make it fail by design once enforcement exists.

title: EnforceKeyExpiry is not implemented and cannot be wired as written
body:
Key-expiry enforcement does not run. `AgentService.EnforceKeyExpiry` now returns `ErrKeyExpiryEnforcementUnavailable` rather than reporting success for work it did not do.

Three independent defects, none of which is fixed by the others.

**1. It asked the repository for zero rows.** It called `agentRepo.List(0, 0)`, which reached PostgreSQL as `LIMIT 0` and returned no rows, so the loop body never ran. Fixed — `List` now rejects a non-positive limit.

**2. The columns it needs are not selected.** `AgentRepository.List` does not `SELECT key_expires_at` or `key_rotation_grace_until`. Both are therefore always nil on every agent the function can see, so `agent.KeyExpiresAt != nil` is never true. Pagination does not change this.

**3. The obvious repair for (2) is a trap.** The function suspends by calling `AgentRepository.Update`, which writes 29 columns while `List` populates a subset. Measured on a real row, that round trip produces:

```
encrypted_private_key    "SECRET-ENCRYPTED-KEY"  -> NULL
key_algorithm            "Ed25519"               -> ""
key_created_at           <timestamp>             -> NULL
key_expires_at           <timestamp>             -> NULL
previous_public_key      "PREV-PUB"              -> NULL
rotation_count           7                       -> 0
capabilities             ["cap:one","cap:two"]   -> null
pqc_public_key           "PQC-PUBLIC-KEY"        -> NULL
pqc_key_algorithm        "ML-DSA-65"             -> NULL
hybrid_mode_enabled      true                    -> false
```

Adding `key_expires_at` to `List`, which is the one-line fix (2) invites, would make the loop reachable and destroy the key material it exists to protect — including the agent PQC public key and the entire capability grant.

## What a correct implementation needs

- A read that carries the key-expiry columns, or a dedicated query.
- A narrow write: `UPDATE agents SET status = $1, updated_at = $2 WHERE id = $3`. Not `Update`.
- A negative test proving an agent with an expired key and no grace window is suspended, and a control proving one inside its grace window is not.
- A decision on whether it should be wired at all. It currently has no caller anywhere, including tests.

## Verify

```
grep -n "key_expires_at" apps/backend/internal/infrastructure/repository/agent_repository.go
grep -rn "EnforceKeyExpiry" apps/backend --include=*.go
```
evidence: EnforceKeyExpiry is not implemented and cannot be wired as written
Three independent defects, none of which is fixed by the others.

title: docker-verify.sh exits 1 with no message when docker compose config cannot interpolate
body:
Running the docker verification gate on a clean checkout produces:

```
  DECIMA Verification Gate
  Branch:  <branch>
  SHA:     <sha>
  Compose: docker-compose.yml
$ echo $?
1
```

No error, no explanation. Exit 1 is documented as "build failed / no compose file / no buildable service", none of which is true.

## Cause

Service auto-detection runs:

```bash
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml config --format json \
  | jq -r "[.services | to_entries[] | select(.value.build != null) | .key] | first // empty"
```

`docker compose config` fails when the env file has not been generated yet:

```
error while interpolating services.grafana.environment.[]: required variable
GRAFANA_ADMIN_PASSWORD is missing a value: Set GRAFANA_ADMIN_PASSWORD in .env
(run ./scripts/gen-dev-secrets.sh > .env to generate one)
```

That message goes to stderr and is discarded by the pipeline; `jq` receives nothing and yields empty, so the script reports "no buildable service". Passing the service explicitly does not help — the next `docker compose ps -q <service>` fails the same way, and under `set -e` the script dies mid-assignment with no output at all.

The compose stack deliberately has no fallback defaults for secret-shaped env vars (CWE-798), and CI enforces that with the compose secret-fallback lint. So "compose cannot interpolate until the operator generates their env file" is the designed first-run state, not an edge case.

## Suggested fix

Probe compose once, up front, and report its own error:

```bash
if ! err=$(docker compose -f "$COMPOSE_FILE" config --format json 2>&1 >/dev/null); then
  echo "docker compose cannot read $COMPOSE_FILE:"
  echo "$err" | head -5
  echo "If this is a missing env file, generate it: ./scripts/gen-dev-secrets.sh > .env"
  exit 1
fi
```

Any exit that produces no output is worth the same treatment — the gate blocks a merge, so a silent refusal is expensive to diagnose.

## Two adjacent findings from the same session

**Compose appends port lists, it does not replace them.** `docker-compose.override.yml` maps postgres to `127.0.0.1:5433`, but the merged config publishes **both** 5432 and 5433, so `docker compose up -d postgres` fails outright on any machine running a host PostgreSQL. Verified:

```
$ docker compose config --format json | jq -r ".services.postgres.ports[]|\"\(.published):\(.target)\""
5432:5432
5433:5432
```

If the override intends to move the port rather than add one, it needs `ports: !reset` before the new list.

**The script passes `-f docker-compose.yml` only**, so `docker-compose.override.yml` is ignored throughout. That is defensible (verify the committed baseline, not local overrides) but it should be stated, because the ports and images it verifies are not the ones a developer sees from a bare `docker compose up`.

title: Capability verifications are recorded as verification_type 'identity', so denials render as failed identity checks
body:
## Summary

Every capability verification is recorded as `verification_type: identity`, so the
dashboard's activity timeline renders a denied capability check as
**"Verification: identity — Status: failed"**. That reads as *the agent's identity failed
to verify*, which is not what happened: the signature verified successfully, and what
failed was an authorization check for a capability outside the agent's grant.

Misreporting an authorization decision as an identity failure is a meaningful problem in
a security product — an operator triaging that row would investigate key compromise
rather than an out-of-grant action.

## Cause

`internal/interfaces/http/handlers/verification_handler.go:423-427` infers the type by
substring-matching the capability name:

```go
verificationType := domain.VerificationTypeIdentity // Default to identity verification
if strings.Contains(req.Capability, "capability") {
    verificationType = domain.VerificationTypeCapability
} else if strings.Contains(req.Capability, "permission") {
    verificationType = domain.VerificationTypePermission
}
```

No real capability name contains the literal strings `capability` or `permission`, so
`http:post`, `web:read`, `fs:read`, `shell:exec` and every other capability fall through
to the `identity` default. The type is only ever correct for a capability that happens to
be named after the word.

## Reproduction

Register an agent with a grant, then send two verifications to
`POST /api/v1/sdk-api/verifications` — one in-grant, one out-of-grant:

```
capability: web:read    -> 201
capability: http:post   -> 403
```

Both rows in `verification_events`:

```
 verification_type | status  |  result
-------------------+---------+----------
 identity          | failed  | denied      <- http:post, out of grant
 identity          | success | verified    <- web:read, in grant
```

Expected `capability` for both; observed `identity`.

## Impact

- The activity timeline shows "Verification: identity / Status: failed" for what is
  actually a blocked capability. The correct information exists in the adjacent
  "Capability Violation Detected" alert, so the timeline contradicts itself.
- Any consumer filtering `verification_type = 'capability'` sees nothing, because the
  column is never populated with that value in practice.

## Suggested fix

This endpoint verifies a capability by definition — the request carries a `capability`
field and the handler resolves it against the agent's grant. The type can be set from the
request shape rather than guessed from the string:

```go
verificationType := domain.VerificationTypeCapability
if req.Capability == "" {
    verificationType = domain.VerificationTypeIdentity
}
```

Alternatively, let the SDK state the type explicitly and treat the substring match as a
fallback for older clients.

## Environment

`ghcr.io/opena2a-org/aim-server:latest`, quickstart compose stack, organization in
`strict` enforcement mode.

comments:
An obvious performance overhead comparison is https://github.com/awslabs/aws-lambda-rust-runtime as they have the same HTTP runtime interfacing constraints.  Rust is a lower level language and should perform better, but we'd like to minimize this gap.

In over 10k events configured at 128MB, split between a "Hello, World" Rust lambda and a "Hello, World" Haskell lambda there are a couple of findings:

The data set is very noisy.

Haskell warm starts have outliers early in their container's life.

Visually, it seems obvious that both Rust and Haskell lambdas can end up running in "fast" or "slow" containers.  Even with n > 10k and outliers removed, we only see a trend p < 0.21 that these two results are statistically different.

If we assume the trend to be correct, comparing fast/fast and slow/slow containers between Rust and Haskell, we see the following results:

Haskell (fast container): 11.2ms +/- 8.1
Rust (fast container): 7.8 +/- 6.8

Haskell (slow container): 27.6ms +/- 18.5
Rust (slow container): 22.5 +/- 17.0

The difference seems to be about 20% in both cases, with similar standard deviation (though with such large standard deviation, _statistically_ we don't have much confidence in their difference).

It still seems that more exploration is warranted, especially at higher CPU allowance.  It seems unlikely to be able to determine the likelihood of hitting a fast/slow container, based on the difficulty to collect the data.  Seems even harder to make any reasonable claim that one language is more likely to fall into one versus another.

title: Cabal file syncing
body:
With the recent migration to GH action, I just noticed that a merge that didn't update the Cabal file _didn't_ break builds that should have been broken.  This makes sense, in that the Cabal builds only view the currently checked in version of the Cabal file, where as stack builds regenerate it.

Notably, however, we publish via stack, which will then regenerate the file.  So in this case, the builds would succeed, but the published version would be broken, which is not good.

One option would simply be to sync things before Cabal builds via something like `stack build --dry-run`.  However, in many ways this defeats the purpose of checking in the file at all.  If we are to check it in, ideally that means that users can use this package with Cabal via git checkout and no additional effort.

It may make sense to abort the build if the generated file were not going to match.  That should theoretically prevent merges that don't keep master in sync.
comments:
I'm thinking of taking this notion even further.

Something that's struck me recently: a version is just an interface.

I think with software today, we see a major conflict between stability and progress over versioning.  Either poor interfaces are maintained forever, or improved interfaces are released and older ones are either abandoned or maintained at great cost.  Though, I have consistently argued that the maintenance cost of multiple versions is lesser than net maintenance generated across the ecosystem in abandonment.  Part of my argument has been that by utilizing `git` effectively, we don't need to pay double the cost for double the maintenance.  However, it's not necessarily intuitive to do this well, and it's not free of pitfalls and its own form of toil.

An approach that might allow us to use something closer to "trunk based development" without abandoning previous versions, would be to have one code based that supports all major versions, where versions only have effect _at the interface_.  For example, the breaking changes introduced in `hal` were fairly minimal.  One exposed function was renamed, and a typeclass implementation was dropped.  If these _top level_ changes are compiled conditionally, the code base between the two versions is 99% the same.  This means that both versions could get bug fixes and refactors more or less for free.  By pushing the interface distinctions out to the edge, most code changes are not likely to involve them.

For the most part, this mostly leaves us with the challenge of metadata.  My thinking is that by using something like `dhall`, we can generate the appropriate files per version supported as needed.  `dhall` would give us the tools to manage conditionals and repetition among them.  These files would be present on a `develop` branch, where primary development would take place.  Then individual release branches and tags would point to code where the cabal files are pre-generated and checked in.  `master` would point to the most recent version.  This would probably leave `hpack` behind, and instead use `dhall` files.

Not sure when I'll have the bandwidth to take this on, but leaves plenty of time for anyone to call this out as crazy :)

title: Difference to aws-lambda-haskell-runtime?
body:
hal was recently highlighted on the Haskell Foundation slack, and got me curious. I am using https://theam.github.io/aws-lambda-haskell-runtime/ / https://github.com/theam/aws-lambda-haskell-runtime for my (few and small) Haskell on Lambda projects, and I wonder how the two related.

comments:
It’s a good question!  One I’m not totally sure how to answer.

Both libs came out at basically the same time, as there was immediate mutual excitement for provided runtimes enabling Haskell—the other was even published a little sooner.  We even had a bit of correspondence about how we might consolidate efforts, but it wasn’t ever quite clear how.

The main goal of this lib was always to enable a bring-your-own-monad approach via Monad Transformers, plus some small adapters that enabled an easier start for when you didn’t want to deal with them.  That opened a door for others to build some cool stuff like the Wai adapter.

I hesitate to speak for someone else’s lib, but the main offering and investment I see is ease of use.  They’ve got some really great docs setup and some things to help bootstrap.

To me, it seems like they both have their use cases.  I think hal may be able to take a user further, but may not be quite as easy for some of the most common cases.

Our goal was just to enable more Haskell, so we’re happy if you use either!

Thanks for the summary! I’ll cross link this to the aws-lambda-haskell-runtime repo. Feel free to close if you like to keep the issue list tidy (or maybe the README should actually have a friendly pointer to the alternative to help new users decide)?

title: Eliminate Possible Laziness Between Executions
body:
#130 address an issue where exceptions weren’t caught in the runtime code because of laziness, but the next step is to try an eliminate this happening in user code too.  There’s little reason for laziness to delay evaluation beyond the current execution—or it should be GC’d, knowing it could never be evaluated at all.

@kokobd, it sounded like your suggestion was to add an `NFData` constraint?
comments:
> @kokobd, it sounded like your suggestion was to add an NFData constraint?

1. For dealing with exceptions thrown in pure functions in user code, there is another way without using `NFData`. At this line: `try (fn (either error id eCtx) event)`, currently we don't call `toJSON` or `Aeson.encode`. If we convert the result to json within this expression, we are effectively forcing evaluation.
2. For dealing exceptions thrown by `hal`'s library code, I suggest a refactor of error handling:
  a. Use explicit `throwIO` instead of `error`
  b. Make error type customizable - not limited to the current `User` error.

Is (1) enough for _all_ possible user code?  I was imagining that if hal code for parsing could get tripped up by this, other kinds of user errors could too.  A user with `error` in their pure runtime likely doesn’t expect that the runtime would exit, and it seems like it would?  I’ve been planning to see if I can recreate this.

The user is free to create any bottom value (infinite list or error) in their data structure as long as it's irrelant for `ToJSON`. After we get the result `Aeson.Value`, no user code will be forced to run anymore, so no new pure error could be thrown. The only other place where the user can throw an error is their `IO` monad, but that is catchable by `try`. So the runtime won't be crashed.

title: Structures for not-just-lambda events?
body:
At work, we're considering using [Lambda Destinations](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/invocation-async.html#invocation-async-destinations) to respond to failed asynchronous lambda invocations. The obvious thing to do would be to PR some new types and `ToJSON`/`FromJSON` instances for that type, but they're not really lambda-specific: they can also be sent to SQS Queues, SNS Topics, or onto an EventBridge Event Bus. So there's a decent case for putting it in some other package

That got me thinking: should we look at separating `hal` from the event types? A package name like `aws-lambda-events` sounds like a fine home for events sent _to_ Lambda Functions (e.g., things that come from an Event Source Mapping) as well as events generated _by_ Lambda Functions (e.g., invocation records sent to a Lambda Destination, regardless of type). And the package would only really need to depend on `aeson` and testing libraries.

I'm interested to hear what you think here, and what namespace we could use to ensure a smooth transition. I expect we'd want to do something clever with re-exports or something so that existing code can keep working with warnings, and then migrate to using the new package as a direct dependency.
comments:
I agree that separating the two is probably a good idea.  The recent move of the Aeson parser was quite a pain for compatibility, so my lean is either to do this soon, or just commit to this being the long term place for events.  I think that's likely not a good idea because I just generally expect that to be a bit more volatile.

So, I think now is probably the best time if more schemas (events or destinations) are of interest.  Based on the Aeson changes, I think flags are the way to go.  It looks like we can add a flag to Hal that keeps event modules out so that they don't collide with the new package. It would default to the existing behavior today, and then maybe eventually we just no longer export them at all in future major version bump.

I'm not sure we need to do too much with flags to ensure a smooth experience for users.

What made things hard in the `aeson` case was IIRC that the package with no modules wasn't initially present, and its lower bounds excluded a lot of previous versions, and it needed `aeson` machinery in its implemenation. This forced downstream packages to use flags. I think we can avoid both of these if we're careful.

What I propose we do:

1. Decide on a namespace for AWS events that's not going to clash. `Network.AWS.*` is pretty full of amazonka <2.0 stuff, so my first thought of `Network.AWS.Events.*` is probably bad. Maybe `Data.AWS.Event.*`?
2. Decide on a package name for events. Maybe `aws-events`?
3. Decide which new version V of `hal` will include phase 1 of the migration
4. Move the event mapping structures across to `aws-events-0.1.0.0`. In version V of `hal`, re-export event mappings from `AWS.Lambda.Events.*` and mark these modules as deprecated.

I think this means packages can move across to `aws-events` at their own pace, and both can be present in the dependency graph without clashing.

We have some types for processing DynamoDB Stream events that we were thinking of upstreaming, but we'll need to do some work on them to make them fit your backwards-compatibility and dependency-footprint goals (namely, they currently depend on [`amazonka-dynamodb-streams`](https://hackage.haskell.org/package/amazonka-dynamodb-streams) to provide some of the internal data structures. While we're here, I was thinking it might be good to split off the existing events and get the AWS events package set up.

Before we went off and did this (in the space between our other work tasks), I just wanted to check in and see what capacity you had to look at and merge PRs, especially since reworking the package structure will be a bit of work.

Also, what are your current goals around GHC compatibility etc? The current release of `hal` declares a `base` bound that implies a GHC 7.something but your Stack configurations only go back to GHC 8.6.5 from 2019.

title: `hal` requires environment variable that are not set by AWS's Runtime Interface Emulator
body:
The runtime interface emulator at https://github.com/aws/aws-lambda-runtime-interface-emulator/ is an AWS-provided way to test Lambda Functions locally. It doesn't set all the environment variables set by the "real" environment, and this causes `hal` to crash when trying to start. The RIE's docs call out the following three variables:

*    `AWS_LAMBDA_FUNCTION_VERSION`
*    `AWS_LAMBDA_FUNCTION_NAME`
*    `AWS_LAMBDA_FUNCTION_MEMORY_SIZE`

There are two more that `hal` expects to be present:

* `AWS_LAMBDA_LOG_GROUP_NAME`
* `AWS_LAMBDA_LOG_STREAM_NAME`

Would you take a PR to make these fields optional?
comments:
It looks like RIE does support setting the first three at least:

> The rest of these Environment Variables can be set to match AWS Lambda's environment but are not required.
>
>    AWS_LAMBDA_FUNCTION_VERSION
>    AWS_LAMBDA_FUNCTION_NAME
>    AWS_LAMBDA_FUNCTION_MEMORY_SIZE

That definitely makes sense to support RIE, but that seems a bit cumbersome to pass the optional handling down to the user of the Context.  Especially when those fields are only not available in a test bench, so they have to have branches in production code for cases that can't occur in production.

I wonder if there's a way to detect if we're inside RIE?  Then we could set them to dummy values automatically.  No impact to production users, but no extra setup for RIE either.

### Describe your problem

The `client_credentials` grant does not support `private_key_jwt` (`client_assertion`) client authentication.

The `ClientCredentialsRequest` struct in `pkg/oidc/token_request.go` already declares `ClientAssertion` / `ClientAssertionType` fields, but `pkg/op/token_client_credentials.go` does not reference them. `token_code.go` and `token_refresh.go` already have the equivalent branch, so the absence in the client_credentials path looks inconsistent.

### Describe your ideal solution


[RFC 7521 §6.2](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7521#section-6.2) explicitly covers the combination of `grant_type=client_credentials` with assertion-based client authentication, so this is a standard feature.

This was previously raised in #813 and answered as "enhancement request rather than a bug", so this issue opens that enhancement request.

The proposed direction is to add a `ClientAssertionType == JWTAssertion` branch in `pkg/op/token_client_credentials.go`, mirroring `token_code.go` / `token_refresh.go`:

- assertion path → verify via `AuthorizePrivateJWTKey`
- otherwise → existing `client_secret` path

title: [Bug]: rp.RefreshTokens drops extra token response fields such as refresh_expires_in
body:
### Preflight Checklist

- [x] I could not find a solution in the documentation, the existing issues or discussions
- [ ] I have joined the [ZITADEL chat](https://zitadel.com/chat)

### Version

v3.47.5

### Describe the problem caused by this bug

## Description

When the token endpoint returns additional fields during a refresh-token exchange, `rp.RefreshTokens` does not preserve those fields on the returned `*oidc.Tokens[...]` / embedded `*oauth2.Token`.

In our case, the OP returns fields such as:
- `refresh_expires_in`

Those values are present in the HTTP response body, but after calling `rp.RefreshTokens`, they are not available through `tokens.Extra(...)`.

From tracing the current implementation, the loss seems to happen because:

1. `rp.RefreshTokens` calls `client.CallTokenEndpoint`
2. `client.CallTokenEndpoint` unmarshals into `oidc.AccessTokenResponse`
3. `oidc.AccessTokenResponse` only models a fixed set of response fields
4. a new `oauth2.Token` is built from that struct
5. only `id_token` is copied into `Token.WithExtra(...)`

As a result, arbitrary extra token response fields are dropped on refresh.

## Expected Behavior

Additional token response fields returned by the token endpoint should be preserved on the returned token and be readable via `tokens.Extra(...)`.

At minimum, this should behave consistently with code exchange paths that preserve extra token response data through the underlying `oauth2` token handling.

## Actual Behavior

Extra fields such as `refresh_expires_in` and others are missing after `rp.RefreshTokens` returns.

### To reproduce

## Reproducer

```go

//go:build reproducer

package review_test

import (
	"context"
	"encoding/json"
	"net/http"
	"net/http/httptest"
	"testing"

	"github.com/zitadel/oidc/v3/pkg/client/rp"
	"github.com/zitadel/oidc/v3/pkg/oidc"
	"golang.org/x/oauth2"
)

func TestRefreshTokensPreservesExtraFields(t *testing.T) {
	srv := httptest.NewServer(http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		if r.URL.Path != "/token" {
			http.NotFound(w, r)
			return
		}

		if err := r.ParseForm(); err != nil {
			http.Error(w, err.Error(), http.StatusBadRequest)
			return
		}

		if got := r.FormValue("grant_type"); got != "refresh_token" {
			http.Error(w, "unexpected grant_type: "+got, http.StatusBadRequest)
			return
		}

		w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
		_ = json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(map[string]any{
			"access_token":       "new-access-token",
			"refresh_token":      "new-refresh-token",
			"token_type":         "Bearer",
			"expires_in":         3600,
			"refresh_expires_in": 123,
		})
	}))
	defer srv.Close()

	config := &oauth2.Config{
		ClientID:     "client-id",
		ClientSecret: "client-secret",
		Endpoint: oauth2.Endpoint{
			TokenURL: srv.URL + "/token",
		},
		Scopes: []string{"openid"},
	}

	party, err := rp.NewRelyingPartyOAuth(config, rp.WithHTTPClient(srv.Client()))
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("NewRelyingPartyOAuth: %v", err)
	}

	tokens, err := rp.RefreshTokens[*oidc.IDTokenClaims](context.Background(), party, "refresh-token", "", "")
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("RefreshTokens: %v", err)
	}

	if got := tokens.Extra("refresh_expires_in"); got != int64(123) {
		t.Fatalf("refresh_expires_in = %#v, want %d", got, 123)
	}
}
```

## Output

Actual output:

```text
=== RUN   TestRefreshTokensPreservesExtraFields
    zitadel_refresh_extras_reproducer_test.go:66: refresh_expires_in = <nil>, want 123
--- FAIL: TestRefreshTokensPreservesExtraFields (0.01s)
```

Expected output:

```text
refresh_expires_in=123
```

title: Make discovery grant and response types configurable
body:
### Preflight checklist

- [x] I could not find a solution in the existing issues, docs, or discussions.
- [ ] I have joined the ZITADEL chat.

### Describe the problem

`pkg/op/discovery.go` currently hardcodes these authorization server capabilities:

- `ResponseTypes` always returns `code`, `id_token`, and `id_token token`.
- `GrantTypes` always starts with `authorization_code` and `implicit`.

A self-hosted deployment can disable implicit and ID-token authorization responses on every registered client, but its discovery document still advertises them. There is no provider configuration that removes those capabilities globally.

This is not a client authorization bypass. Clients that only allow `code` correctly reject `response_type=id_token` and `response_type=id_token token` with `unauthorized_client`. The problem is that the server metadata overstates the deployment policy, and operators cannot publish code-only metadata without maintaining a fork or rewriting the discovery response at a reverse proxy.

OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice recommends authorization code instead of responses that issue tokens from the authorization endpoint. Some security reviews also require discovery metadata to match the enabled deployment policy.

Relevant code:

- https://github.com/zitadel/oidc/blob/main/pkg/op/discovery.go
- `ResponseTypes` includes a TODO about making the values dynamic.

### Describe your ideal solution

Add provider configuration for server-wide supported response types and grant types, with current behavior as the backwards-compatible default.

When configured as code-only:

1. Discovery returns `response_types_supported: ["code"]` and does not advertise `implicit`.
2. Authorization requests using `id_token` or `id_token token` are rejected at the provider level, even if a client is accidentally configured to allow them.
3. The same configuration drives metadata and request validation so they cannot drift.
4. Existing deployments that do not set the new options retain the current defaults.

A possible API would add `SupportedResponseTypes` and `SupportedGrantTypes` to provider configuration, then have both discovery generation and authorization request validation consume them.

### Version

Observed with `github.com/zitadel/oidc/v3 v3.47.5` in current ZITADEL main. The hardcoded behavior is also present on the current `zitadel/oidc` main branch.

### Environment

Self-hosted

### Additional context

- RFC 8414 defines these discovery fields as the grant and response types supported by the authorization server: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8414.html#section-2
- RFC 9700 recommends authorization code instead of implicit responses that expose access tokens in the authorization response: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html#section-2.1.2

We currently enforce code-only behavior per client and have live negative tests for both ID-token response types. Configurable server-wide enforcement would remove the need for a discovery rewrite at the edge and protect against future client misconfiguration.

title: Proposal: single config-struct constructor for RelyingParty (and ResourceServer) client construction
body:
## Summary

This is a proposal / discussion-starter, not a demand for a specific implementation. I'd like to get a maintainer/community read on whether it's worth simplifying how `rp.RelyingParty` (and by extension `rs.ResourceServer`) clients are constructed, before I go build something that depends on the current shape.

## Problem

[`rp.NewRelyingPartyOIDC`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/zitadel/oidc/v3/pkg/client/rp#NewRelyingPartyOIDC) has this signature:

```go
func NewRelyingPartyOIDC(ctx context.Context, issuer, clientID, clientSecret, redirectURI string, scopes []string, options ...Option) (RelyingParty, error)
```

`clientID` and `clientSecret` are positional constructor arguments. But an alternative credential — JWT Profile authentication — is bolted on afterwards as a functional option: [`WithJWTProfile(signerFromKey SignerFromKey)`](https://github.com/zitadel/oidc/blob/v3.49.2/pkg/client/rp/relying_party.go#L384) (and the deprecated `WithClientKey`).

In practice this means:
- When JWT Profile auth is used, `clientSecret` has to be explicitly passed as `""`, even though it's semantically "not applicable," not "empty."
- Credential/identity configuration (which secret material authenticates this client) and purely behavioral/integration configuration (`WithHTTPClient`, `WithErrorHandler`, `WithUnauthorizedHandler`, `WithCookieHandler`, `WithPKCE`/`WithPKCEFromDiscovery`, `WithAuthStyle`, `WithVerifierOpts`, `WithCustomDiscoveryUrl`, `WithSigningAlgsFromDiscovery`, `WithLogger`) are both expressed through the same `Option` mechanism, even though they're conceptually very different — one is "who is this client," the other is "how should the client behave."
- Building a `RelyingParty` from *declarative* configuration (e.g. a config file or database row describing a provider) is awkward: the caller has to inspect which credential shape is in play and route it to either a constructor arg or a specific `Option`, rather than just populating one struct.

## A positive precedent already in this repo: `pkg/client/rs`

`pkg/client/rs` (resource server / introspection) already avoids this problem — but via a different mechanism: separate constructors per credential shape, each taking exactly the params it needs as positional arguments:

```go
func NewResourceServerClientCredentials(ctx context.Context, issuer, clientID, clientSecret string, option ...Option) (ResourceServer, error)
func NewResourceServerJWTProfile(ctx context.Context, issuer, clientID, keyID string, key []byte, options ...Option) (ResourceServer, error)
func NewResourceServerFromKeyFile(ctx context.Context, issuer, path string, options ...Option) (ResourceServer, error)
```

Only genuinely behavioral options remain as `Option`s there (`WithClient`, `WithStaticEndpoints`). `rp` has no equivalent per-credential constructor — everything funnels through one constructor plus `Option`.

## Proposal

Consider a single config struct that carries **all** identity/credential fields (issuer, client ID, client secret, JWT-profile signer/key, redirect URI, scopes, ...), constructed directly — something like:

```go
type Config struct {
    Issuer       string
    ClientID     string
    ClientSecret string        // mutually exclusive with JWTProfile in practice
    JWTProfile   SignerFromKey // or equivalent
    RedirectURI  string
    Scopes       []string
    // ...
}

func New(ctx context.Context, cfg Config, options ...Option) (RelyingParty, error)
```

Purely behavior-changing, integration-facing options (`WithHTTPClient`, `WithErrorHandler`, etc.) stay exactly as they are today — functional options are the right tool for those. The struct only replaces the "which credential material authenticates this client" part of the surface.

Two open questions I'd like input on rather than assert an answer to:

1. **Where should this live?** Given `rp.NewRelyingPartyOIDC`'s existing signature can't change without breaking every caller, would it make sense for this to live in a **new, standalone package** within the `oidc/v3` module (e.g. something like `pkg/client/rpconfig`, or scoped as a v4-style package) specifically so it can be introduced without a breaking change to the current `rp` package?
2. **Should it also cover `rs`/introspection?** `rs` already has the multi-constructor-by-credential-shape pattern this proposal borrows from. Should a new config-struct-based client extend to resource-server/introspection construction too (either the same struct, or a parallel one), so both client types get a consistent construction story? Or is `rs`'s existing per-credential-constructor approach good enough as-is and this proposal should stay scoped to `rp`?

## Motivating use case

We (ZITADEL) are exploring defining SSO/IdP provider templates (Google, GitHub, etc.) as static, embedded config files (YAML/JSON via `go:embed`) rather than hard-coded Go, specifically so adding a new provider template doesn't require a Go engineer and a code change (see [zitadel/nextgen#851](https://github.com/zitadel/nextgen/issues/851) and its follow-up proposal issue). Turning such a template into a working `RelyingParty` is significantly simpler against "populate one struct" than against "positional args plus figure out which options apply to this provider's credential shape."

## Ask

I'd like this issue to serve as a discussion thread to reach a conclusion on: is this worth doing as a refactor/addition to OIDC, or is the existing constructor + functional-options shape good enough that downstream consumers (like the use case above) should just adapt to it as-is? Happy to help prototype a standalone package if there's appetite for the former.
